I am the bearer of good news. This is not a world record, but it is approaching it. In view of the fact that from a few feet you can get a commercial oil well, members of this house can well imagine the tremendous and favourable effect of the news which has been received. EXPRESSION OF WELCOME ON ENTERING CONFEDERATION
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, since I have the honour to represent in this house the only constituency whose territory is neighbour to that of the new province of Newfoundland, I wish in the name of my constituents to extend to our fellow citizens, especially those of the Labrador coast, the most hearty welcome on the occasion of the entry of Newfoundland into our confederation.
During the last seven years, in the course of my visits to the extreme eastern part of my riding, I have had occasion to meet a good number of Newfoundlanders who already have had very close and friendly relations with our own people. Having had the opportunity of knowing them, I am sure they will become good Canadian citizens.
Many residents of the north shore are the descendants of settlers who came to our country from Newfoundland. That is the reason why the ties already existing between the people of the two countries will be tightened by the joining of Newfoundland to the other provinces.

We were good neighbours. Now we shall become members of a single family and it will be our desire to work together for the prosperity of a great country.

speechtext:
1.	Are permits available to enable parents or widows of Canadian service men whose graves are in the British or American zone in Germany to visit such graves?
2.	If so, what is the procedure?
3.	If not, would the government give consideration to granting issue of such permits?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PERMITS FOR NEXT OF KIN TO VISIT WAR GRAVES OVERSEAS
speechtext:
1.	Permits are not generally available for
the specific purpose of visiting war graves. Recommendations may, however, be made to the military permit offices of the occupying powers in especially compassionate circumstances. Application in such cases may be addressed to the Department of External Affairs, Ottawa.
2.	Answered by No. 1.
3.	It does not lie within the competence of the Canadian government to grant permits to enter the occupied zones of Germany. The government, however, has on a number of occasions brought to the attention of the competent authorities the desire of Canadian relatives to visit war graves. Advice is now awaited from the government of the United Kingdom as to whether it will be possible to develop arrangements by which visits may soon be made to graves in the United Kingdom zone. While it is understood that military permit offices will not generally grant permits to the United States zone for the specific purpose of visiting war graves, it may nevertheless be possible for visitors to enter the United States zone as tourists under certain prescribed conditions laid down by the United States zone authorities.

speechtext: I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Although I have no brief for the people concerned, has the minister any comment to make on the recent summary ejection of two Canadian citizens from the United States? Further, has the government, or any member of it, received a letter concerning this matter from a nonpolitical and certainly noncommunist group of Canadians attending Columbia university?

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
The hon. member was good enough to give me notice of this question, which I think concerns an incident in New York last week end affecting three Canadians who were removed by United States authorities from a banquet which they were attending in connection with the so-called cultural and scientific conference for world peace which was being held in that city. The United States authorities have of course every right to prevent Canadians and others from entering their country. They have every right to deport Canadians and other foreigners who are in their country. We claim that right ourselves. However, in view of the fact that the circumstances surrounding the exercise of this right in the case of the three Canadians in question seem to have been, to say the least, unusual, and in view of the fact that only Canadians appear to have been interfered with at the banquet in question, I thought it desirable, when I noticed a reference to this matter in the press, to request at once a full report on the situation from our embassy in Washington and from our consulate general in New York. That report has been received, and I am examining it to see if any further action seems to be required.
Our interest in these persons was solely in the fact of their being Canadian citizens, and must not be interpreted as indicating approval of any political views they may
Inquiries of the Ministry hold, or endorsing in any way the conference they were attending.
As to the second part of the question, a letter was received this morning from Canadian students at Columbia university protesting against what they called "the highly arbitrary treatment of Canadian citizens on the occasion in question".

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question? Were these three so-called Canadians communists? Has the minister any information in that regard?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: The three Canadians were Professor and Mrs. Barker Fairley, of Toronto, and John Goss, of Vancouver. I am not in a position at the moment to make any statement about their affiliation or otherwise with the communist party. There is evidence to support the view that at least some of them did have connection with the Labour Progressive party.

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: Were they not deported because they were said to be communists?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Why were not communists from other countries treated in the same
way?

subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: I should like to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs if it is a fact that the three Canadians referred to as having been ejected from the United States were not so ejected because they were communists or reputed to be communists?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: DEPORTATION OF CANADIAN CITIZENS FROM UNITED STATES
speechtext: The three Canadians in question have not been ejected from the United States. One remains in that country, as a special lecturer at Columbia university. I would also point out that we have not questioned in any way the right of the United States authorities to deport anyone from their country. Nor have we protested in respect of this particular incident. All I said was that the circumstances surrounding the incident seemed to call for a report, if we could get it, from the United States authorities. We have received that report, and we are now deciding whether further steps are necessary.

I wish to address a supplementary question to the Minister of Agriculture. Can he tell me what the situation is with regard to fish meal? I understand that a similar shortage exists in that type of meal.
I answered by saying that I would take the question as notice. In answer to the question the following information is submitted.
On the Pacific coast the herring fishing season has just ended. Compared with the past two or three seasons, little herring was canned, the catch being used for oil and meal. Almost 31,000 tons of fish meal has been produced, which is the highest on record. Supplies for the markets served by Pacific coast fisheries are good. Prices remain firm, indicating that demand is also good.
Atlantic coast fishing is more or less continuous, the main outlet for the catch being the production of fillets. However, the heaviest fishing season is during June, July and August. Fish meal is produced from the scrap remaining after filleting, and the production is up considerably from the previous season. Supplies are at least equal to average, but firm prices indicate that demand is absorbing the output.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in opening this debate some ten days ago I referred to the cyclical nature of the budget and pointed out that it followed a political not an economic cycle. I pointed out that there should have been tax relief a year ago but that the minister preferred to save up and present us with a lemon last year so that he could cut a melon this year. I referred to the fact that, whether or not there were employment projects, there were certainly electoral projects. I said that it seemed clear that it was not the needs of the taxpayers but the needs of the party opposite that was calling the tune. I said that the taxpayers had got what could only be called partial restitution. I called the budget a bribery budget and I said that the taxpayers would have little difficulty in seeing through this obvious vote-catching device.
This was in sharp contrast with what the minister had said. Abandoning his usual modesty the minister with a great flourish of trumpets boasted of various things. He pointed out that the tax reductions during the last five years totaled something like $1,300 million. He then referred to the reduction in the debt to which I shall refer a little later. He also made mention of various social security measures and wound up by saying, "I know of no country in the world that can show a better record."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Apparently there are some hon. gentlemen opposite who agree with the minister. I was surprised at his manner until I realized that of course this was the minister's swan song, that he had seen the writing on the wall, that he realized the government was being weighed in the balance and found wanting and that
2180	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell this was his last chance to claim fame before the curtain fell.
I am an accommodating person. If anyone feels that the word "bribery" is too blunt, I am ready to offer certain alternatives.
I imagine that the minister is a clever angler, coming as he does from the eastern townships, and I suggest that he was astute in baiting the hook for the taxpayer. In these days when the Irish sweep is in everyone's mind, perhaps I might use a phrase from the turf and say that the budget is by Political Necessity out of Suffering Taxpayer.
I do not propose to take any more of the time of the house in referring to what I call these election projects. I would only remind the citizens of Cape Breton, and the veterans of Hong Kong, who have received long deferred and inadequate recognition of their services, that they are fortunate that this is an election year, because otherwise they might have had to wait long enough for their just deserts to be remembered by the government.
I now come to the question of tax reduction. I must frankly say that I think the minister did his best to spread the jam as far as it would go. We have an offering to small corporations; we have an offering to shareholders; we have an offering to the general body of income taxpayers; and we have reductions in various excise taxes. I said in my opening remarks, and I say again, that I particularly approve of the relief given to small corporations if that measure can be so devised as to be free from abuse. It seems to me that it is a very useful thing, because we need small new enterprises constantly coming into being in order to maintain our free system.
There is one thing that the minister did of which I cannot approve, and that is the increase in the normal corporation tax from 30 to 33 per cent. It seems to me that this is clearly a breach of faith with the provinces. The minister may say that perhaps the written wording is capable of some other interpretation, but I say that this kind of thing would not be done in the relations between individuals, and it should not be done either in the relations between governments.
As to excise tax relief, the minister has covered a lot of territory. We have jewelry, luggage, traveling bags, and, for the benefit of those who are mistakenly called the weaker sex, we have relief on cosmetics. There is relief for smokers, of which I myself do not approve because I am not a smoker.

Then there is a further device which I am sure, Mr. Speaker, must have gladdened the minister's heart, and which I am sure he regards as his ace of trumps. I refer to the retroactive feature, which made certain reductions retroactive to the first of January. If we look back to two years ago when the minister gave tax relief, it was not made retroactive then. It was put forward; it did not come into effect until July 1. Of course, Mr. Speaker, that was not an election year, and so there was no particular need to put it back. In fact it would have been rather a nuisance to put it back, but now the minister has learned and, of course, the political wheel has turned, the political cycle has arrived, and the minister feels that cash on the barrelhead is the thing. He may have heard of the remark attributed to J. P. Morgan when somebody in his presence referred to "cash or its equivalent." That great financier said, "There is no equivalent for cash." I think the minister may have had that in mind.
The minister realizes that the taxpayer will be not only pleased but also surprised to see his money making a return trip. I think there is no doubt that the minister must have thought that was a good one, that the taxpayer would actually be having money paid back to him. I want to remind the minister of one thing. Do not let him forget to put in that blue slip which says, "this comes to you with the compliments of the Liberal party".
I think we may assume, Mr. Speaker, that, when the minister started collecting dollars to go vote hunting, he scraped the barrel, because after all he was concentrating on the election. He was not worrying very much about what will come afterwards, and indeed I think that the fellow who comes into power afterwards may find that the cupboard is very bare.
His estimate of income for the year 1949 is based on the assumption that everything will go well. We have got to have good trade, good crops, no labour troubles.

speechtext:
The
minister ignores the fact that there are certain storm signals flying abroad. In the United States things are not just as rosy as they were. It looks as if the boom was subsiding a bit, and if it does do not let us fool ourselves-it will affect us in Canada because we are more vulnerable by reason of the extent of our foreign trade.
As I say, the minister scraped the barrel, and he has found as much beneficence to distribute as he possibly could. Of course, we welcome tax reduction, and our complaints are only two. The first is that it was delayed until this year, and secondly we complain that it was in part wrongly distributed. We say that the minister ignored the needs of the group of taxpayers between $2,000 and $2,500 for married people and $1,000 to $1,250 for single people. We feel that this group is entitled to a higher priority. We feel the same about additional allowances for children. Last autumn our convention went on record to that effect. We did so deliberately, and after as careful investigation as we could make. We stand by what we did then.
Therefore we say that this group of taxpayers is in greater need than some of the others. For example, while it is a very nice thing that people who are traveling should have the tax taken off their tickets, and that people who use long-distance telephone service should have the tax taken off their accounts, we do not believe that their need is as great as that of the group I have mentioned. After all, a married man with an income of $2,200 a year has not very much left for traveling after he has paid for the necessaries of life, and he does not use the long-distance telephone very much. Therefore we say it would have been fairer if that group had been considered and given a higher priority.
I could mention other items in the excise group which we think might have waited. I believe further that some of the income tax relief which has been granted is not as much needed as relief to the group of taxpayers I have mentioned. If this was true last October when we passed our resolution, it is truer now because government policy has added somewhat to the cost of living of the class I am talking about. I say that some regard should have been had for those who have been hit hard by such things, for example, as the increase in the cost of bread. The particular class to which I have referred for which we appeal, and all other nonincome tax payers, outnumber all income tax payers. Therefore there is no reason in the world why they should not have been considered more than they were.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
Another point I wish to make is that if relief had been given last year, and if the surplus this year had been the result not merely of continuing high taxes, but of doing a certain amount of saving, then the government might have been in a better position this year than it was in order to meet the needs of these people. We might have had more economy. But how can you have economy when everyone in the government service knows that there is a huge surplus?
Economy is not in the air; spending is in the air. We all remember the immortal remark made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I blush to repeat it, but after all it was an immortal remark, made some three and a half years ago when someone on this side asked if a million dollars-could not have been saved. "Yes," he said,, "we could have saved a million dollars, but what is a million dollars?" That was when we were having a deficiency in our national income. Imagine what the minister would say if he were asked that question now, with surpluses running into the hundreds of millions.
I ventured to tell the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) last year that he would never get any economy until he rationed the various departments; but how can you ration departments when you have a surplus which in the last two years, including certain special figures, ran not far short of $2 billion? 1 do not suppose the ordinary head of a department can believe in the existence of such a thing as economy when he knows there are these hundreds of millions of dollars to play about with. And it seems to me just human nature, Mr. Speaker, to say, "What are a few tens of millions of dollars as against two billions or even $575 million?" Philip Snowden was right when he spoke about the danger of these surpluses, because when there are piles of money by way of surplus no. one is going to think very seriously about economy.
I think it is a great injury to have this-situation arise. Debt reduction, yes; of course we want debt reduction. But we do not want it in a hit-or-miss fashion. We do not want it just as the political cycle turns, but we want it on a sensible basis, regularly carried out and known to all.
To show how absurd the thing is, Mr. Speaker, I have only to point to the contrast between 1948 and 1949. I have tried to put it in the form of a simple algebraic equation; it has to be simple or I would not understand it. 1948: good times plus large surplus minus election equals debt reduction but practically no tax reduction. 1949: good times plus large surplus plus election equals tax reduction
2182

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell without debt reduction. You see, it is like one of the simplest propositions in Euclid, one of those near the first of the book; but what a light it casts upon the refusal to give any reduction last year, and the keeping of it all until this year.
I said, and I repeat, that I think the minister made a genuine, honest attempt to spread the jam around as far as he could, and to ingratiate himself with as many people as possible. I confess that as I listened to him at first I was a good deal impressed; as I mentioned, I feared the appeal to cash, and I thought the taxpayer, even when he knew it was his own cash making a return trip, might be pleased and, for the moment, led away. But the more I have had a chance to reflect on this budget the more it seems to me there are great gaps. The jam was not spread everywhere; there are great holes in the net; many kinds of people were not -aught in it.
As I say, in spite of the minister's genuine attempt, in spite of the glee with which he told us how good his timing was, there are these oversights.
Moreover, I think the electors are becoming cynical, and I even wonder-though of course the minister would never admit this-whether "he has sometimes wondered if it would not 'have been better to give some relief last year, as he should have. At any rate, I am inclined to think that more and more taxpayers would accept the reasoning contained in a rather /good cartoon which appeared in the Toronto 'Telegram the other day. I hope the minister lhas seen it, because it is really very flattering. The minister is shown with a most insinuating and ingratiating smile. He is under the eye of a policeman-

I heard a report of what a man in western Ontario had to say about this budget, and I have summarized it because it seems to me to describe the position very well. He said that the Abbott budget contained sunshine for all classes except the very large class- and as I said a moment ago I believe it represents the great majority of the people-who are scrimping along through the high cost of living period in the low income bracket, where income tax reductions do not mean anything at all. This man then refers to the increase in the price of bread.
Then I had a report from Nova Scotia which was very similar. There are many nonincome taxpayers in Nova Scotia, too, particularly in the country, and there they are interested largely in flour and tobacco. Apparently this man is a bit of a wit, for he said, that when the taxpayer first saw this budget he thought it was pretty good; but when he took a second look at it he said, "Santa Claus filled the stocking but stole the Christmas tree." This same authority in Nova Scotia points out that the cost of feed has jumped, with bran up 20 cents and barley meal up 25 cents. So the dairy farmer finds himself between the upper and nether millstones, with higher costs and lower prices for his butter.
I have dealt with the effect on the taxpayer. Now I am going to deal briefly with the reasons mentioned by the minister for no relief last year. I feel sorry to have to take time on this, but the minister went to considerable trouble to explain it and it seems to me I should not wholly disregard that part of his speech. Of course it would have saved a lot of trouble for both the

The minister began to give this explanation: "A tax reduction last year would have come too early to be of real value-" and at that point he was interrupted by loud and sustained applause from this side of the house. It was only after some little time, and after the ovation had subsided following this unintentional revelation of the truth, that he was able to add, "to be of real value to the public as a whole."
It is only fair to the minister to say that he gave a much more elaborate explanation than that. I am now going to give you that explanation. Mr. Speaker, and I am sure you will be greatly interested in it. As reported at page 1794 of Hansard he said this:

I know what they would say, but I do not think I should repeat it here. I think they would have been still more annoyed if they had known that the minister went on to say, as reported at page 1794 of Hansard:
To have reduced taxes then-

On
rainy days, as the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Hackett) points out. What I want to point out is that even then battle was in the air. The minister had smelt the scent of the election battle. And when he used the phrase "keep our powder dry", of course what he was saying was, "we have got to keep this money available for next year."
Now we come to 1949. On the face of it, it is extremely similar to 1948-prosperity practically unprecedented. Of course that was the story in 1948. But the action is

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell entirely different. As I told you, in 1948 we had to put away for a rainy day; we had to keep our powder dry. But now in 1949 there is little or no debt reduction. One important reason given by the minister was this. He says we have paid off $1,600 million in the last three years. In a sense I think that is true. I think it is probably quite accurate to say that we have paid off creditors to the extent of $1,600 million. But I want to point out, Mr. Speaker, that this reason, although apparently solid and sensible, is largely illusory when you come to examine into the thing.
There is, I believe, an old adage, which says "save at the spigot and let out at the bunghole." If you look into this matter further, you will find that while we were paying off our creditors with the one hand, we were busy making some $1,200 million of advances with the other. Where did those advances go? They went to the United Kingdom and to other European countries, and I am glad that they did. But I do not believe that there has been anything but a moderate reserve set up against them. I do not believe the minister, even in his most optimistic moments, would tell us that we are likely to get that amount back in any foreseeable time, because I am sure the minister would be only too glad if he thought we could import enough goods from those countries in the next few years to pay for the goods that we would like to sell them in those years, apart from getting a lot of goods to make up for the advances which we have made.
But, Mr. Speaker, it is really wasting your time to deal with these economic considerations because, as we know, the minister had other and more weighty reasons in his mind. Last year, after all, we had no election and we could have an economic slogan: Tax and tax, pile surplus on surplus. This year, with an election in prospect, we have a political slogan: Cut and cut, elect and elect.
Let me emphasize that we are not objecting to the reduction. What we are objecting to is that it was not given last year, and that it is saved up to the eve of an election for this highly improper purpose.
Before I leave this attractive subject I just want to indicate that really the minister finally comes around and makes it unanimous by agreeing with us, as I shall show you in just a moment. After all the hair-splitting and tight-rope walking, the minister finally slipped and fell into the real explanation which appears at page 1795 of Hansard. where he says this:
Finally, sir, I should say that I have been led to believe in recent months-


Note that, Mr. Speaker: in recent months. -as no doubt other hon. members have, that most of the Canadian people would support and even welcome an enlarged measure of tax reduction this year.
Fancy that, Mr. Speaker. He has learned that in recent months, he says. The only question I can ask is this: Where were his ears all those other months? The answer is, I think, that the minister must have a deaf ear and that he must have turned that deaf ear obstinately to the people who were trying to tell him the truth. So there, Mr. Speaker, you have it plain and flat. The minister joins us and makes it virtually unanimous: the election is the thing that unlocks his heart.
I have been dealing so far with what we will call the vote-catching technique of the government; but I do not believe that the voters of this country are going to decide how to cast their votes in the next election on the basis of any handout given at this time, a little of their own money given as an act of deathbed repentance. I do not believe that the voters of this country are like that. I think they are going to judge the government by its capacity to administer their affairs.

The
doctor says: "That is just wishful thinking." He apparently would not like to have that test applied.
The minister told us in that little modest outburst the other night that the government had been skilful, intelligent and prudent. That is an interesting claim and we shall examine it. I think everyone will agree, Mr. Speaker, that while we can adopt several criteria, the best criterion of all would be to take the way they have dealt with trade, because after all trade affects us all. Even the minister, when he is off guard, admits that foreign trade is in a rather precarious position. The trade question is the greatest challenge that faces the government. I suppose we can say, to copy Mr. Micawber, that if foreign trade is good the result is happiness, but if foreign trade is bad the result is something not far from misery.
Let us see what the Minister of Finance said about foreign trade. First he referred to trade with the United States which he said was favourable. In a way it is, although I shall have something to say about it later. Speaking about our export trade he said, as reported at page 1787 of Hansard:
We cannot be satisfied with its present situation or immediate prospects.
Further on he said:
To the extent that . . . markets are closed to us, we must develop alternative outlets.

Again he said:
We must persevere in working out the constructive solution through trade agreements on a wide nondiscriminatory basis.
In one of the school plays I read I remember that somebody made a remark and the answering comment was, "good sentences and well pronounced." We can say that to the minister, but at the end of it I would feel like saying: "So what? What do you do about it?"
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is a hearty fellow. He says that Canada is on top of the world. Our gross national product is up a billion dollars over 1948, and as a result of a survey by his department, barring earthquakes, serious labour management troubles, or a change in government, he adds prudently, Canada can be assured that 1949 will be as prosperous as was 1948.
The Minister of Finance has some fears about external trade, but apparently the Minister of Trade and Commerce has none. I must admit that his opinion is a little discounted by the fact that he did not seem to know that any payments received for exports to Europe last year were as a result of the Marshall plan. When he was asked about that he just said he did not know from what source the money came. That struck me as rather odd. I think I told him the other night that since he was the man who was selling our products he might well have taken a little more trouble to find out where the money was coming from.

Actually I think the minister did himself an injustice when he said that. I think he knew more than he admitted. I believe it was one of those careless statements he makes, because he does not take the house too seriously. He does not really think that he need take very much trouble to answer our questions. I can only say that I hope he will do better next time, if there is a next time, as I am reminded.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had something to say about it. First of all he said in London:
I am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can be expected to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed to interfere with the will of those who have empty stomachs.
That seemed a sort of down to earth statement. I hoped that the minister would follow through on it, but I was a bit disappointed, because speaking here in this house, and telling us about the agreements which had been made, he was rather complacent about the situation. Later on, again speaking about the converting of sterling into dollars and dollars
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell into sterling, he seemed to indicate that he thought we could do nothing about it, though he admitted that it would cause a little trouble in marketing our products. In the end his only suggestion seemed to be that if our customers were in difficulty we could go on financing them. Well, that is good. We have done a lot of it. It is an argument which I think every sensible man should keep his ear open to, but it does not seem to me to be any solution. It is only a palliative for the present situation.
Where does this leave the government? I suggest that we have had no real statement of the gravity of the situation. To do the Minister of Finance justice he hinted at it. Of course the Minister of Trade and Commerce just brushed it out entirely and there is no indication of any action. All we have are these vague phrases which we get from the Minister of Finance, amiable phrases, well meaning phrases, but no coming to grips with the matter. It seemed to me that the whole thing was reminiscent of a phrase which was in common use a good many years ago, and which some people who have the misfortune to be as old as I am can remember. I refer to a famous phrase attributed to the late Lord Oxford, "wait and see".
After these rather vague and milk-and-water statements, if I may say so, without causing offence to anyone, I should like to ask the house to listen to a rather fresh voice speaking from the outside world, speaking, as they used to say in the air force drill, loud and clear. This is a statement by the able correspondent of the Financial Post, and which is dated March 26. He says:
The harsh effects of economics are splitting the democratic world into two. As the United States. Canada, and their western Europe partners move closer together politically in the contract of the North Atlantic pact, there is an ever-widening economic gulf separating America and western Europe.
Ironically enough he says, in a way the Marshall plan has had the effect of demanding that they help themselves. He goes on to say:
So the friends across the Atlantic have been encouraged. if not indeed coerced, into minimizing their purchases for dollars and into increasing their trade with each other.
And again:
They're doing so well in enlarging trade among themselves . . . that they've . . . pulled down the currency curtain over the Atlantic.
He points out the difficulties which result from sterling being a high cost area. For example, he says that Britain pays thirty-two cents to thirty-four cents a pound in sterling for Argentine hides, against a price in the United States of twenty-four cents; that formerly Australia used to be Canada's third

The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell largest outlet for newsprint, and that she is now required to buy Scandinavian newsprint at a price of $60 to $70 a ton above the Canadian price. That is all because of the exigencies of being in the sterling area. On the purchaser's side he points out that, whereas we used to buy nearly all our coffee in the sterling area, now, owing to the price differential, we have to buy it from the dollar area. Therefore the thing pyramids on itself and gets worse and worse. He also quotes the authoritative London Economist on this question of the high cost sterling area. This is what the Economist says:
Prices may be falling in the world markets, but the price of British imports continues to rise, because British purchases have been concentrated for currency reasons on the dearer markets.
Again he quotes from the Economist:

After referring to one favourable factor, namely, that Britain is buying ninety million board feet of spruce in eastern Canada, which is a 50 per cent increase, he winds up by saying that on the whole the overwhelming evidence is unfavourable.
Then he asked this searching question, which I pass on with all the earnestness I can to the government: "Do we in Canada try to sit it out while our trade dries up before our eyes?" Again he asks, "How long can Britain and other non-dollar countries continue to hold their present currency levels?" And he answers, "Nobody knows."
Then he concludes with these challenging paragraphs:
The stimulus of Marshall aid Is driving Europe into its own trade shell, not out of it. Right now only a few are conscious of this danger and its fatal implications to multilateral world trade. Very soon the implications of this situation will dawn in the minds of millions of people in our North America whose livelihood and well-being depend upon the outcome.
Now, these blunt words, coming from a well-informed source, seem to me worthy of careful consideration, as against the rather veiled hints mixed up with Pollyanna optimism which is coming from the other side of the gangway. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), judged by his words, knows nothing except prosperity unlimited. And I would be much happier if he had not spoken in such an unlimitedly optimistic manner.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) knows better, but he does not seem to do much except utter these amiable generalities.
I should like to bring this situation a little nearer home. Only the other day I spoke to a man who came from the West Indies just two or three months ago. This is what is happening in the West Indies-and it is not
[Mr. Macdonnell (Muskoka-Ontario).J

the least bit amusing. Our trade was something in the neighbourhood of $15 million before the war, and it grew during the war to nearly $60 million, because during the war we supplied them when nobody else could or would, and they came to look to our market. They liked us, and would like to continue trading with us. They have four and a half million people. But what is the situation? Our trade has now diminished to a beggarly $3 million, and even that is the result of a small concession given by the colonial office so that our Canadian products could go in there on a kind of token basis.
These are the illustrations I wish to give. They like our products and would like to trade with us, but they are in the grip of the sterling area. They want our flour, but they cannot have it. They have to take Australian flour. My friend ran into a businessman who was using Massey-Harris implements, and wanted more. At first he could not get them at all. Then he finally found a way of getting them. Where did he get them? He got them from Australia, not from Canada. Massey-Harris operates in Australia. He was not able to get them here.
As I said a moment ago, we have now got a slight concession, just a toe in the door. But while this sort of thing goes on the situation gets worse and worse.
Let me give one other illustration. In Port of Spain my friend went into a retail shop in which he found a man who said he wanted to sell Canadian shirts, but could not. He had to sell British shirts at 50 per cent higher because of the exigencies of exchange.
He visited the Dominican Republic, which is at the opposite extreme. The Dominican Republic is a hard-money area. As a matter of fact they look down on the Canadian dollar. They condescend to take the American dollar at par, but not our dollar. But the interesting thing there was in connection with apples. My friend found that apples cost 20 cents each. He asked whether any attempt had been made to get Canadian apples, or whether their sale had been pushed. He is an ex-Nova Scotian, and he pointed out that Nova Scotian apples were a glut. Upon asking whether anything had been done to push Canadian apples in the Dominican Republic the man with whom he was talking replied that he did not think so. In that I think that his informant was quite right, because I find that in the year 1948 apparently we sent only one hundred barrels of apples to the Dominican Republic.
In the face of this there is very little comfort to be had out of the minister's general statements-as I have read them. He says, "We cannot be satisfied with its present

situation or immediate prospects"; "we must develop alternate outlets"; "we must persevere in working out the constructive solution through trade agreements."
But all those generalities do not grapple with the main problem which is, as we know, restoring the convertibility of the pound. I am not going to resume the debate we already have had respecting the foreign exchange control board, but I do mention this point because it is most relevant. I say again, as I have said before, that on this the Minister of Finance is defeatist; and that until we have convertibility of the pound restored, which we hoped to accomplish two years ago, as will be recalled, all the other things are palliatives; and the longer the sterling area remains as the high-cost area, the worse the situation becomes.
I do not think it is an exaggeration to say that unless effective action is taken in that direction there is just no reason to believe that we can keep up our sales of products in western Europe at anything like their present level. Though the Minister of Trade and Commerce ignores it, our trade at present is maintained very largely by the Marshall plan.
Therefore I come back to this and when the minister boasts, as he does, about our rigid dollar, and all the government's skill in finding the ne plus ultra level at which to maintain it, I remind him that in order to maintain that he has had to establish quotas against the United States and other countries. In other words he has had to add fuel to the very flames he is trying to quench.
One other point. The minister talked a good deal about favourable trade with the United States-and that is all to the good. But do not let us forget that it is not on as firm a basis as we would like. In boom conditions all kinds of things "go." You can do business under boom conditions which cannot be done under other conditions. But there is a great deal of reason to believe that the boom is fading, and if that happens our markets will be affected in the United States. If that happens another need will arise about which we did our best to persuade the government during the debate on the foreign exchange control board. We will need to have American investments in this country, which have rescued us when we were in trouble several times before.
That brings me to what I said before about convertibility and about getting on toward freedom of exchange, and taking the steps which we urged upon the government to try to move the international monetary fund toward a broader base. I wish merely to repeat that the fundamental basis of the government's action is negative.
The Budget-Mr. Macdonnell
Happily not everyone is negative. We find that Hoffman, who is distributing Marshall aid, is not negative. He asserts that there should be realism in this matter, and Snyder of the United States treasury says the same thing. They take a constructive attitude. It seems to me a grand opportunity was offered to Canada, but up to the present time the government is not taking it. So I say I believe the government is failing to grapple with this situation, and that by its behaviour it is landing us in a mess.
I doubt very much whether the minister, or any other minister, will undertake to argue with the Canadian taxpayer that on the government's dealings, on their handling of the foreign trade situation, they are entitled to the votes of the Canadian electors at the next election. It would be easy to give other instances, but I do not propose to do so at this time.
Mr. Speaker, what are we to do in the face of a budget like this?

Are
we to approve of the fact that the government refused a tax reduction a year ago by reason of its election requirements and kept the taxpayers out of their money?
Are we to approve of the fact that in this budget the whole farming community has been denied any real relief, in spite of rising costs in connection with some of their necessities?
Are we to approve of the fact that nothing has been done for the very large class who are scrimping along in the low income brackets, who are non-income tax payers, and who, far from having relief under this budget, have their costs of living actually increased at the present time?
Are we to approve of the intellectual gymnastics of the Minister of Finance as we try to follow his explanation of when we reduce taxes and when we do not? Perhaps the best we can say of this is to use Churchill's phrase that "It is a riddle wrapped in a mystery inside an enigma."
I do not propose to confine my criticism to this or that point in the budget. My criticism is of the budget as a whole and of the government which approved it. What I criticize is the whole attitude of the government as shown by this budget which is full of inconsistencies and, what I think is worse, wanting in constructive power and equally wanting in the courage to face and grapple with the great dangers which face us.
It is the budget of an old and tired government which has produced rabbits successfully out of hats in the past and hopes that

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell now in extremis it can succeed in doing it again. But this time it is too late; I believe the hour has struck.
Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith):
That all the words after 'that" to the end of the question be struck out and that the following be substituted therefor:
"This house is of the opinion that the government does not possess the confidence of the country."

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before proceeding with my remarks on the budget itself I should like to join in congratulating the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon the excellent way in which he delivered his budget statement. I think the house generally appreciated both the manner of its delivery and the style of the speech.
I want also to congratulate him upon having included in this budget a few elements of tax reduction which we have urged during the past years and which we feel were necessary and wise, particularly the raising of the income tax exemption levels in so far as they went.
I should like to thank the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) for the announcement he made this afternoon that farmers may now charge as a cost the value of what they pay their children for their labour. I think this should be allowed whether they pay or not, and I think also that a wife's labour should be considered. We have urged that in this house on many occasions during the last number of years.
As we moved in our amendment last year, as we felt then and as we do now, in view of the removal of controls, in view of high prices generally and high rentals for homes, then, as now, prevailing, we feel that the minister should have accepted the proposals made last year by the C.C.F. party-incidentally I would remind the official opposition that they were not supported at that time by the official opposition, either by vote or by speech-that the exemptions in the lower brackets should be raised to $1,250 for a single man and $2,500 for a married man. May I remind the official opposition that the reason we did that was the high cost of living, which in great part was due to their insistence upon the removal of the beneficial controls and subsidies which had been in effect during the war. Frankly, Mr. Speaker, my congratulations are going to end there.
A careful reading of the budget will show that the optimism regarding Canada's economic outlook which was expressed by the minister is, we think, not justified. Indeed a careful study of his speech will show that the minister does not really share the optimism which he expressed in this house the other evening. In neither present conditions,
fMr. Macdonnell (Muskoka-Ontario).]

nor the outlook for our country's economy, nor indeed the over-all nature of the budget proposals, is there anything about which this house or the people of Canada can really cheer.
Last year I said that the annual budget presented to parliament should be more than a mere outline of the government's receipts and expenditures. It should be a survey of our national economy, explaining present difficulties and pointing to dangers that may be appearing on the horizon. Having done that it should lay the basis for economic prosperity and progress in the years that follow.
We consider that at the present stage of development a national budget should include a national plan for the maintenance of full production and high employment. It should include provisions to enable the distribution of goods and services to, and their enjoyment by, all our people in a manner which would be both just to the producer and fair to the consumer. At this time it should also lay the basis for that comprehensive and integrated system of social security which the Canadian people need, but lack.
The present budget does none of these things. It seems to have been based, as has already been said, on a survey of the electoral needs of the Liberal party. It certainly is not based on a survey of the economic and social needs of the Canadian people. In short, it is a traditional, political, capitalist budget which makes a few concessions to the lower income group since they have many votes. But the main benefits of the budget go to the well-to-do who will gain most by the kind of tax reduction which the minister announced. In addition, the wealthy investors are given appreciable benefits by the concession on the taxation of dividends. It should be noted that the only indirect taxes removed are those on luxuries, such as the excise tax on jewelry and so on.
The burden of the hidden eight per cent sales tax which hits the farmer and the poorest section of our population the hardest is again left untouched. I remind the government that when the sales tax was raised in the 1930's by a Conservative government the Liberal party was bitter in its criticism of what some of their leading critics described as a most pernicious tax. This afternoon we listened to the leading critic of the Progressive Conservative party denouncing a tax which his party used to excess during the 1930's.
It is therefore significant that when the Liberal party is in power it maintains the highest sales tax ever known in the history of the country. Indeed the budget shows an alarming tendency to rely more and more on

hidden and regressive tax measures such as the sales tax. With complete frankness the minister admitted that in pursuing this course he was following the line of least resistance. As reported on page 1795 of Hansard, the minister expressed the belief that the income tax on individuals was the fairest and best tax to have. He then went on to say that the public does not like a level of income tax sufficient to meet our requirements so he was retaining substantial taxes on goods and services and taxes on corporate profits. In other words, because most of the public are unaware of the onerous nature of hidden taxes such as the sales tax they can be retained as a principal source of our country's revenue.
Those are not courageous nor are they admirable reasons for a wrong social policy. I think it is the duty of this party to protest and to enlighten the people of Canada on every possible occasion regarding the heavy burden borne by the poorest section of our population because of this sales tax. Finally there is conclusive evidence in the budget that the government has abandoned all pretence of planning for the future. The demands of big business, voiced in the house so largely by the Progressive Conservative party, and by powerful sections of the press which support them, have had an effect. Nearly all beneficial controls and subsidies are off. Profits are to govern unchecked. The future and well-being of our people are back in the clutches of monopolistic industry and finance. The lesson of the past is forgotten so that, if we face the possibility of an economic breakdown, there remain no plans or machinery to halt it should it come. Surely no one will deny that there are many great and urgent problems facing Canada today, and it is the duty of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget to deal with them as best he can through that medium.
The time at my disposal is limited, but I wish to discuss at least four of our major economic problems. They are first, and perhaps the most pressing, the present and possibly future loss of many of our export markets, particularly for our agricultural and natural products; second, the prospect of a not too distant collapse of our capital expansion boom with the consequent threat of another serious depression, and unemployment; third, a general falling off in the standards of living, of which I shall endeavour to provide some instances; fourth, the disastrous effects of high prices and inflation over a period of years on pensioners and others living on relatively fixed and low incomes.
To take them in turn and indicate the magnitude of the problems which should be tackled without further delay, I want to 29087-1391
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell refer first to the precarious position of our export markets. In the early part of his speech the Minister of Finance spoke of "the three major catastrophes, war, crop failure and widespread industrial stoppages." Let me add to the list another major disaster which may occur, namely, the situation which will result if we fail to reverse the present trend in the overseas marketing of our agricultural and natural products.
The minister is budgeting for a surplus of $87 million this year. Yet at the same time he suggests that we may need more than $200 million to finance our exports, an amount which I cannot find in his budget. He further suggests that we may have to borrow money in the fiscal year beginning tomorrow because his cash surplus of $202 million may not be enough to meet the country's needs. This is certainly a reversal of the principles laid down in the minister's budget speech of last year. Then we were told that the government was following a policy of cyclical budgeting under which substantial surpluses could be accumulated in good times to meet a possible deficit in bad times.
I know, of course, that the Progressive Conservative party has urged the minister time and time again, in season and out of season, to get rid of the surplus, and to stop preparing for a rainy day. Apparently they have convinced him that this is a good policy for an election year, although I was very interested this afternoon to hear their critic taking exactly the opposite point of view.
In order to maintain our overseas markets for the huge surpluses which we cannot consume in this country, we must do everything possible to encourage imports from countries which are our traditional customers, and particularly from the United Kingdom. Such a policy is certainly essential for the welfare of Canadian agriculture, and the C.C.F. will urge it and support it to the fullest extent. The government is now pinning its hopes for trade on a return to multilateral trading. That is a fine ideal, but the world economic-situation makes its attainment impossible at the present time. It is, therefore, not a practical trade policy for Canada at this moment. As long as convertibility of currencies remains impossible, Canada must maintain any volume of trade by adopting the forms of trading relationships which her customers require.
This means that bilateral agreements by our country are necessary to maintain our volume of trade. Our best customers are planning their trade through long-term agreements and bulk purchases by government agencies, merely because the world situation is such that they must do that in

The Budget-Mr. Coldwell order to get the supplies that they need. Of course this is a new pattern of world trade made necessary by present conditions, and we should not permit doctrinaire adherence to unworkable ideas to retard the prosperity of Canada's basic industries. That is exactly what I feel the government is doing in regard to trade.
Let me say that whenever convertibility is possible again I believe that an attempt should be made to promote world-wide trading relationships as freely as possible. But we are not within reach of convertibility. In the meantime, therefore, I believe we must do all in our power to build a larger and more balanced trade with the sterling bloc, and particularly with the country which has been our best customer for years, the United Kingdom. Is the government doing this? On the 18th of May last the Minister of Finance announced the extension of British preferential duties on cotton and rayon piecegoods to June 30, 1949. I want to quote a sentence from what he said at that time. It reads:
There will be an opportunity to review this whole matter on the basis of results achieved before that date.
But in his budget speech ten days ago, while the minister said, "I am not proposing any tariff changes at the present time," yet in his very next sentence he announced that he was not asking parliament "to extend the special temporary provisions regarding the duties on cotton and rayon piecegoods. These will expire on July 1, 1949." Surely this involves a very important tariff change because the removal of the British preference becomes effective on the first of July of the current year.

Surely this indicates that good progress was made during the past year, but in spite of that the British quota for textiles was not reached. Under the circumstances it would seem to be prudent to extend the special arrangements for another year to encourage the further expansion of British exports to Canada in order that they can obtain the necessary dollars with which to buy Canadian products. I repeat that such a policy is essential to Canadian agriculture. Yet what does the government do? It cancels the special encouragement to Great Britain and then goes on to increase the quotas generally giving other countries a larger share of the market before our best customer for agricultural products has had an ade-
IMr. Coldwell.]

quate opportunity to re-establish herself in this, her long-term pre-war market. I suggest a further extension be granted.
I believe that the government should also investigate spreads in prices of British goods after they reach Canada. There has been a great deal of criticism of the high prices of British textiles in Canada. We have been informed by people who were there that in Winnipeg a British trade representative stated that a woman's suit, available from the manufacturer in England for $45-I presume that would be made from utility cloth -costs the Canadian consumer $125 when laid down in this country. That is something which, if true, should be looked into. If spreads of this sort are permitted it is no wonder British textiles are expensive in Canada.
Then I should like to say one further word about trade. The European recovery program will not last forever. That is noted in the budget speech, of course. What will Canada do when ERP ends; or indeed-and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is anxious about this-if the United States should declare wheat a surplus commodity? We may be protected for a year or so, but after that, what? That is what we who represent prairie constituencies are asking ourselves. So I say it is parliament's responsibility, indeed the government's responsibility because it must give the house leadership, to prepare now for any of these eventualities and not wait until 1952. But the budget presents no proposals to meet any of these difficulties should they arise. [DOT]
The next major problem to which I wish to direct attention is the government's failure to do anything to control the capital expansion boom. In 1945 some five per cent of our gross national expenditure was devoted to capital investment. In 1948 this figure rose to twenty per cent. A high level of capital investment is desirable at times, but we need to examine closely the kind of expansion that has been taking place in the past year or so. There is a desperate need for housing, though the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Winters) was quoted in the Montreal Gazette of Tuesday last as declaring that there is no housing emergency in Canada. Let me remind him that there are few people in Canada whose incomes are sufficient to buy or rent a house valued at $15,000 or to pay, as you must in this city, $100 a month or more for an unfurnished one or two bedroom apartment in an apartment block. I notice one of the ministers pointing to himself and indicating that is what he is paying. In that case he should have some sympathy for the plea I am making. The minister of reconstruction

had better not repeat his statement of last Tuesday or he will undo for the Liberal party everything they evidently expect to gain by the introduction of this budget.
Most people are fully aware that the need for housing constitutes a real national emergency and a threat, I may remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), to national health and welfare in this country. What we need, Mr. Speaker, is a low-rental housing plan; and in spite of the opposition of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to subsidized housing, reported a year ago, we shall have to provide it. I can assure you that if the people of Canada elected a C.C.F. government we would undertake it immediately.
Housing is needed, too, in our rural areas. This was brought out on March 17, when in reply to a question asked by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) the house was told that section 15 of the National Housing Act, which was designed to benefit rural housing, had not been put into effect because of the "continued scarcity of certain building materials." What an excuse that is when in every city across Canada, including this city, we have seen the construction of theatres, breweries, bowling alleys, and commercial construction of all kinds. The shortages that have denied decent homes to our farmers and other people are caused by the building boom in luxury homes and commercial enterprises. Earlier in the session we were told, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Nicholson), that up to the end of 1948 only one farm home had been built under the National Housing Act. The government policy, too, has permitted industry to centralize itself more completely in Ontario and Quebec at the expense of the west and of the maritime provinces. The government should have stipulated-and incidentally they did this in the United Kingdom- "No breweries, no theatres, no luxury building, no unnecessary commercial expansion will be permitted until we have made substantial progress in solving the housing problem and have built hospitals, schools and other badly needed public facilities." By the system of priorities in effect during the war something similar was done quite successfully and could have been continued while this grave national housing emergency lasted.
This is an example of what we mean when we say that both the government and the official opposition put profits ahead of human need as the guiding principle of their economic policies. Direction must be given by a national investment board, too, responsible to parliament; for fluctuations in capital investment over a period of years will spell disaster for the nation once again if it proceeds along
The Budget-Mr. Coldxoell the lines we have seen during the past year or two.
I wonder if the minister realizes that during his budget speech he referred twelve times- I counted them-to the "uncertainties," the "difficulties" and so on which face Canada in the near future. It is interesting to note that he used the word "uncertainties" five times in the course of his remarks. I have already drawn attention to some of these uncertainties. The Canadian Statistical Review tor February, 1949, pointed to the decline in real consumption by the consumers of this country in 1948. A month ago I asked for the per capita expenditure on consumer goods and services in each of a number of years, based on the dollar valued at its pre-war level, because this seemed to me to be the best possible index of the trend in the overall standard of living of this country. What do the figures show? They show that the real consumption per capita dropped by four per cent from $521 to $501 in terms of pre-war dollar value, as between 1947 and 1948. The minister spoke of producing a record quantity of consumer goods, but the figures show that, if we are producing more, we are consuming less. Surely this should be the red light indicating that we are not able to distribute that record production among our people. It indicates the failure of Canadian capitalism once again.
. During the past three years average wages have followed the cost of living-and I say "followed" and I mean "followed"-fairly closely; but the position of pensioners and persons on fixed incomes has sunk. Old age pensioners, for example, in spite of increases by both the federal and provincial governments, today have a value of not more than 95 cents expressed in the value of the 1945 dollar; but according to government statistics corporation profits have actually risen 75 pec cent since 1945.
There has been much discussion regarding: the factors which have caused the enormous-price increases since 1945. Let me point this out. Of the total charged by business for things produced in Canada, twelve per cent consists of corporation profits and ten per cent of indirect taxes. In other words, twenty-two per cent or almost one-quarter of prices is made up of profits and indirect taxes. Who benefits most from such an unjust balance in the economy? Certainly not the farmer; certainly not the consumer; certainly not the great masses of the people. Yet in face of this, excess profits taxes have been abolished.
In 1947 the minister said that profits before taxes were running at an abnormally high level and he added that, if business conditions were normal, competition and bargaining would reduce profits to normal levels, and.

The Budget-Mr. Coldweil under those circumstances repeal of the excess profits taxes would be justified. The tax was repealed in spite of rising profits in the economy. At that time, in 1946, profits stood at $1,421 million. Now the latest figures for 1948 show corporation profits at $2,174 million. This figure, incidentally, can be found in the appendix to the minister's own budget. The same figures indicate that the profits after taxes are up thirty-three per cent from one year ago. If profits were abnormally high in 1947, what are they now?

speechtext: They are fantastically high now.
