speechtext:
There has been neither competition nor bargaining to reduce them. They are the results of monopoly and certain shortages. Let me remind the house that the C.C.F. was alone in demanding the retention of the excess profits tax. Had it been kept, greater social services or greater tax reductions would have been possible now.
Now of course the Progressive Conservatives are expressing their opposition to a small increase in the tax rate of corporation profits which have been raised on amounts of over $10,000 but only affect profits over $77,000. The minister boasted that the income [DOT].tax had been reduced by $177 million since 1945, but he reduced the excess profits tax Sby $466 million when it was discontinued.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario *(Mr. Macdonnell) read part of a letter. I should like to read a letter I received the *other day. I think it is a good statement of the effect of this budget and of government ipoldcy on pensioners and persons with fixed tow incomes. This is what the writer says:
Am writing you to register a strong protest against the budget just brought down.
I am retired and consider myself lucky to have a small pension of $45 per month. There are, however, thousands of Canadians who get less than that and no doubt thousands more who get none at all and who have to depend on their meagre savings to see them through until they attain the old age pension age.
It was with eager anticipation that we waited to hear the details of the budget, hoping against hope that we would hear of some tax relief for our forgotten group, such as the removal of that iniquitous 8 per cent sales tax, elimination of the postage tax (we write a lot of letters) and the tax on tobacco (most of the men smoke even if we can't afford to). What a disappointment we got, when the details were finally revealed. There was not one single item of relief to us in the entire budget. In fact we are worse off than ever, as the price of bread has now gone up, on account of subsidy on wheat toeing removed.
While it is appreciated that the lower income taxes will benefit the small wage earner, it does us no good as we never had any income tax to pay. Then the luxury tax! Can you imagine any of us buying these items? Tax on railway fares, et cetera, mean nothing to us, nor does removal of taxes on soft drinks, chewing gum and candy bars, as we *cannot spend any of our small pittances on such as that.

It is hoped that I have made myself clear. I could not resist the impulse to write you ... I might add that we are looking forward to the coming elections.
Last year I described the budget as a "vinegar" budget. This year it has already been referred to as a "slot machine" budget. Besides the fact that the minister had seen fit to reduce the tax on slot machines, the whole procedure of taxes and tax reduction indeed looks like a slot machine. For ten years all Canadians have been playing the game of putting so much in the federal treasury in taxes, while cabinet ministers have said that some time we might get something back. But when the day came, as in all slot machine operations, some gained and some lost; and those who lost were like my friend the pensioner, whose income is so small that he did not receive enough to pay a tax, even on the level of low exemptions. But they have to buy bread like millions of others; they cannot get along without it.
I wish therefore, Mr. Speaker, to move a subamendment to the amendment already moved. Seconded by the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), I move:
That the amendment be amended by inserting therein, after the words "this house", the following words:
"regrets (a) the failure of the government to remove the sales tax; (b) the action of the government in removing the subsidy on flour milled for domestic purposes, thus adding to the cost of living, and (c) the failure of the government, despite rising national income, to make any provision to improve the living standards of the millions of Canadian people compelled to live on income below the income tax exemption levels, and therefore . . .
And so on.
When parliament endorses this budget, the increases in the price of flour will affect every farm home where bread is baked, and every city consumer who buys from a bread wagon. Today in this city an announcement was made that the price of bread would rise from one to three cents a loaf in a day or two.
For years the western farmers subsidized the bread of this country. That subsidization was an imposition upon the wheat grower. Then for a brief period the government took over the subsidy and subsidized it. Now both the farmer in his consumption of flour and the people in their purchase of bread will be penalized.
If we examine the income tax changes, we find that they are not as generous as they appear to be on the surface. The minister said, as reported at page 1796 of Hansard:
Tonight I propose still further substantial reductions in this tax-
That is income tax.
-in the form of both reduced rates and Increased exemptions.

Everyone knows that increased exemptions have the effect of reducing taxes for all who pay income tax. But the budget does not reduce the rates in all brackets.
Last year the lowest rate was ten per cent. This year it is fifteen per cent. Actually the government has failed to give the first $500 of taxable income the consideration it received last year. I would appeal to the government to reconsider that matter and to make the tax as it was in that respect last year.
At the end of his budget the minister dealt with the Liberal record in the present parliament. He made a pre-election speech. A careful scrutiny of the Liberal record will show that the greatest tax relief has gone to big business-not this year but throughout the years-which is enjoying record-breaking profits, as I have already said-up seventy-five per cent in three years.
The least help in the way of tax relief has been given to those on low incomes-those who have been hurt most by the increased cost of living in which indirect taxes, the sales tax and the dropping of beneficial subsidies and controls have played an important part.
In the field of government expenditures, we note that old age pensions, family allowances, veterans' pensions and so on have not kept pace with the diminishing value of the Canadian dollar. No prevision has been made for health insurance, and the lack of a sizeable surplus prediction exposes the fact that the government has no intention of doing anything further about this problem in the foreseeable future.
I have no doubt that we shall hear health insurance promised again in the forthcoming election, just as it has been in every election since 1919, when it first appeared in the Liberal platform. The people should not forget that we have had thirty years of promises and little action. That is the Liberal record in this respect.
I have no time to go into the Conservative record which, with all their present promises, is a record of opposition to many of the social services that we now have in effect.
In his budget the minister said we are getting back to normal levels of tax revenue. If this is true and the budget speech indicated uncertainties, and indeed the end of the present boom, it becomes clear that no major increases in social service benefits or indeed for national defence, if we require it, will now be possible without increased taxes in the future.
Hence I assume that no matter what the Minister of National Health and Welfare may have promised, the Department of Finance has decided it shall not be fulfilled.
The Budget-Mr. Coldwell
No provision is made for subsidized housing. We can subsidize gold but not housing, milk or bread. What a strange sense of values is indicated in the government policy.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, may I say that while we welcome the few good features in the budget, we look beneath the surface and, seeing what is there, we must condemn the policy behind it.
Before I take my seat may I repeat that the Canadian economy, vulnerable in so many respects, is not helped by this budget. The farmers, and the people engaged in the production of natural products who must find markets overseas, will find little hope in this budget for them. The withdrawal in some respects of the slight advantages which have been given to the United Kingdom at the present time is a further barrier against the sale of our apples, of our salmon, and of our natural products. In almost every field in which the producer who works with natural products is concerned, grave unsolved problems confront us. Therefore I say that we of the C.C.F. must condemn the policy presented to this parliament in the 1949 budget.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Before I launch into a discussion of the budget I should like to direct a complimentary word to the lady member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum) on bringing into this house this afternoon some much needed colour. We like her new Easter bonnet.
Just a word or two, Mr. Speaker, relative to the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). It is almost identical with the type of amendment or subamendment which we would have moved had it been possible for us so to do, and naturally we shall support the subamendment.
During the past two months since parliament opened I have sat and listened to the proceedings with a great deal of interest, and I came almost to the conclusion that the Tories had caught the Whigs in swimming and had made off with their clothes; but the night of March 22 was a great night for the Whig team. Ernest Thayer would doubtless have described the scene in this house that evening in this manner:
There was ease in Abbott's manner as he stepped into his place,
There was pride in Abbott's bearing and a smile on Abbott's face;
And when responding to the cheers he lightly doffed his hat,
No stranger in the house could doubt 'twas Abbott at the bat.
Perhaps the resemblance to the famous Casey ceases at that point; perhaps it does not, but at any rate I should like to congratulate the hon. gentleman on the very healthy cuts he made at the ball, even if

The Budget-Mr. Low
there are many people who thought that he took three healthy swings and struck out. My personal opinion is that he was pretty much out of practice this time. He had two strikes against him already. In my judgment, had he tried a few cuts at the ball last year the chances are that he would have had his eye on it this time and he would probably have belted a home run and probably would have brought his whole team home to score. About the best that I can say now is that he might possibly steal home as a result of a pop fly and a couple of errors.
It is possible that this will be the last budget to be presented by the hon. member for St. Antoine-Westmount. I did not say that it is probable, mind you; I say it is possible. For that reason I am going to be just as generous as I possibly can in dealing with it. Most certain it is that the reversal from the previous policy of the minister proclaims in pretty loud language that this will be the last budget in this very interesting and historic twentieth parliament.
I approve the new trend of the budget, the new look. It provides some basis to hope that the Liberal government is beginning to yield to the insistent demands of the people for the results that the people are entitled to and that they want from the management of their affairs by their government.
We of the Social Credit group, Mr. Speaker, sincerely hope and trust that before this parliament is prorogued the trend that I have noted and mentioned will find a much more complete realization than it has found thus far in the budget itself.
I do not share the horror which has been described by some hon. members on this side of the house as having seized them because the new desirable trend in the budget stamps it quite positively as a pre-election budget. I declare that that trend is long overdue. This twentieth parliament, sir, is now in its fifth session. In each of the four preceding sessions this Social Credit group, which I have the honour to lead in this house, has consistently placed on record its criticisms of current budgets. In every single instance we have offered constructive alternatives to the proposals of the Minister of Finance. Had our proposals been heeded by the administration, then the needs of the electors of this country would long since have been recognized and satisfied to a degree far exceeding the limited, I say very limited, recognition that the Minister of Finance placed before us on Tuesday evening, March 22.
Our proposals are on record in Hansard session after session of this twentieth parliament. They are on record in Hansards of the nineteenth parliament, the eighteenth parlia-

ment and the parliaments ever since 1935 when my friend, the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore), valiantly led this group. In all that time there is not on record a single attempt, much less a successful one, to establish by logic and reason, on a basis of fact, that effect could not be given to what we proposed in the way of financial reform calculated to bring relief to the electors in a measure far outstripping anything that has now been proposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott).
Our proposal for a national dividend, for compensated price discounts and tax reduction is on record again this session in the debate in reply to the speech from the throne. But that does not mean that we are not delighted that at long last a move is being made in the right direction. And, what is more, we take quite keen satisfaction in what is implied by the fact that this change of granite ministerial heart comes to the administration as they have to face the electors in an election.
Why should there be satisfaction on our part in this? I will tell you why. In no nation in the world has integral democracy yet been realized. By that I mean democracy in politics, in economics and in social institutions. To some degree we admit that we in Canada do enjoy political democracy. We are lucky in that, too; because during the past few years we witnessed the collapse in nation after nation in Europe of even that degree of democracy which we now enjoy.
That is why I say it is heartening to have in the minister's budget something of tangible evidence that here in Canada the people still have some hold on the process by which they can demand results from those who administer public affairs in the federal field. To the extent that that is manifest in this budget and elsewhere, to that extent we rejoice in what remains to us of government of the people, for the people and by the people.
It seems to me there ought to be a lesson in this for the Canadian people. It should occur to them that if governments and representatives are prepared to listen to orders at a time when those representatives have to face the electors in a general election, then the people ought to find some way of estab-. lishing constant effective control over their government and over their representatives, so that they will listen to orders all the time.
Social Credit philosophy emphasizes the need for that kind of effective control by the people; and Social Credit policy provides just that. When that policy is applied in our national life we will have established in Canada true political democracy. Our progress can then be real and constant, instead

of spasmodic as it is today. We can then establish economic democracy; and I say we cannot until that time comes.
I think a taste of what was awaiting the Liberal administration, and what may yet be facing that administration, came from the people in the Ontario provincial elections last year. The Liberal party took a beating then. And the vote in that election as well as that in several by-elections since was a vigorous protest against last session's budget presented by Casey when the second strike was called against him.
I congratulate that group of six or more Liberal members, including those from Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt) and the then member for Algoma East, and others, on bringing in a quite forceful manner to the Minister of Finance the facts of the situation as they then obtained. I feel sure their protests, along with some others, perhaps contributed in some measure to the change of heart we have witnessed in the past year.
That is all to the good, of course. I was pleased, too, to hear quite a number of members on the government side of the house during the recent debate in reply to the speech from the throne bringing home to the Minister of Finance the needs of this time-although I must admit that I wondered why they waited until this late date to voice their demands on behalf of the people. I think all members in all parties, singly or in groups, should not hesitate to take every honourable means within their power to bring home to the government the needs of the Canadian people at any time.
I hope I can count on groups on this side of the house, as well as on the other side, and even upon the minister himself, to sponsor some of the proposals I shall make today as a result of my study of the minister's budget. In my contribution to the budget debate of 1948 I commented upon and protested against a tradition which had grown up through the years, through all the parliaments since confederation. I regret that this tradition seems to have fastened itself upon the house. May I repeat that protest now.
I refer to the assumption that a budget, once it is presented to the house, is immutable and unchangeable, and that the prestige of the administration is bound up in the observance of that tradition. I believe that is not a good condition for Canada. No minister of finance can possibly be great that way. If the minister and the government were willing to accept sound proposals for changes calculated to bring greater good and happiness to a much larger number of Canadian people, then they would rise to a degree of greatness rarely achieved by ministers of
The Budget-Mr. Low finance in the history of the world. I do not care from what side of the house such proposals come, so long as they are calculated to bring greater good to a greater number of Canadian people. If they are good, then I believe the minister and the administration ought to be ready to enact them.
Relative to this point, it was with considerable satisfaction that I heard the minister's comment when he was speaking of the difficult problems he faced in finding an equitable method of dealing with the taxation of long accumulated surpluses of family corporations. His reference, as reported at page 1800 of Hansard, is in these words:
I am not prepared to make specific proposals for enactment at this session of parliament. I hope that there may be an opportunity of having a plan of the type mentioned discussed when we are in committee.
I take it from what the minister has said that if an accessible plan is forthcoming as a result of those discussions in committee, no matter from what side of the house it comes, it will be enacted at this session. To do so, I suggest, would be a most desirable expression of confidence in parliament as a whole, something new and refreshing that would raise the prestige of parliament as an institution. Particularly would this be so if the spirit to which I have referred, to a reasonable and sensible degree, would underlie the presentation of all proposed enactments, no matter from what side they may come.
We are too prone to be bound by party traditions, and it is not good. With this in mind I ask now to turn to a discussion of certain specific items in the budget, and more particularly to some which are not included. I cannot deal with all of them. The budget is a comprehensive review, and necessarily I must limit myself to certain specific items. My colleagues, I take it, will deal with other matters which I do not mention.
I would say that no measure is likely to contribute more to a realization of general proposals made in the speech from the throne than enactments proposed in the budget speech. In this session therefore I think it should be expected that the budget, more than anything else, would pave the way to a realization of that very commendable and desirable objective set out in His Excellency's speech from the throne, where he said:
It is the view of my ministers that a steady advance towards the goal of social justice for all is an effective safeguard against the influence of subversive doctrines.
That is a most worthy statement of objective. We Social Crediters prefer to call for social justice to each and to all. I think that in those circumstances where justice is said to be provided for all that the forgotten man must most endure.

The Budget-Mr. Low It seems to me that the feature of this budget is limited increases in exemptions from income tax and still more limited reductions in rates. We all appreciate these things very much, but as the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell) has said, it is merely giving back something that has been taken away by highway robbery methods. We realize that communists in this country would call the minister's budget a bourgeoisie budget, and I think that was emphasized somewhat by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). We believe that it is very wide of the mark in bringing to realization the proposed objective in the throne speech, namely, to safeguard against the influence of subversive doctrines by extending social justice to all. Let me remind the government that communism thrives on setting up the proletariat against the bourgeoisie, on contrasting the condition of the labouring, producing, underfed, forgotten, low-income peoples, the classes that were never able to secure or to earn enough to be included in any income tax bracket, the all too numerous classes in this country, with the idle bourgeoisie. This budget plays right into the hands of the communists and the lines of their propaganda.
Not one particle of consideration is to be found for the poor among the poor, for the labourer, for the farmer; all the consideration seems to be for the middle and upper income groups. Why in the name of common sense does the Minister of Finance continue to impose the heavy burden of the eight per cent sales tax, a tax which is imposed at the manufacturer's level and which bears so heavily against the poor? There is no relief for them whatever. Year after year we in this group have fought this uneconomical and undesirable tax because we know that it pyramids costs so much that it burdens the consumer beyond his endurance.
Sales and other hidden taxes increase the cost of living and force the workers of this country to demand increased pay. That in turn results in further increases in the cost of production and pushes up the everlasting spiral of the cost of living. The minister expects that he will get from the sales tax something like $400 million in round figures, but I venture the assertion that it will cost the consumers of Canada not less than $600 million. That works out at the rate of $50 for every man, woman or child or $200 for the average family of four. I realize of course that every family of four would not pay that much through this hidden tax because the poorer families are so limited in the volume of what they can purchase. However, it is a burden on these poor people out of all proportion to the burden upon any other income group.

We declare that the lower income groups in our country must be given relief at this session if this parliament is to give any substantial recognition to the idea of social justice for all as an effective safeguard against the influence of subversive doctrines.
The sales tax could and should have been abolished last year. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech attempted to build up a good argument to show that it would have been unwise to have given substantial tax reductions last year. The main burden of his argument was that the supply situation then was such as to make reductions in 1948 a dangerous thing. But the sales tax was one impost that could have been removed last year without the slightest danger, even with the supply situation as it was. The removal of the sales tax by the government would have made possible very substantial reductions in the cost of living to people in all income groups. The inflationary pressures would therefore have been eased somewhat. I feel perfectly sure that the minister cannot refute that statement.
This year of course several methods of giving relief to the Canadian people presented themselves to the mind of the minister and no doubt they combated strongly in his mind for preference. The minister could very well have given the same increases in exemptions as are provided in the budget. But if instead of the reductions in the rates that remained he had slashed into the sales tax he would have succeeded in giving fair relief to all income groups in our society without in any way endangering his budgetary position. I repeat most emphatically that by so doing he could have given material assistance to a most needed reduction in the over-all cost of living. I do not intend to burden this point here because I have mentioned it in several speeches already during the session.
This is one most important omission which the people of this country are going to remember and that recollection may cost the minister and the government very dearly when they face the country at the forthcoming election. If the sales tax is not to be removed at this session, and even if it is, then justice demands that at least old age pensions be increased with the means test removed, and that some reasonable consideration be extended to the disabled. In addition, subsidies should be provided for items like bread and milk. Already the price of bread has increased in various communities across the country as a result of the removal of the subsidy on miller's wheat. Milk increased one cent per quart yesterday in a number of communities. We protest most vigorously against the removal of the subsidy on miller's wheat for Canadian consumption. It seems to us to be a queer kind of result from a

budget that seeks to disarm communist propaganda and to achieve the desirable objective of social justice to all.
I noted from the press last night that the minister of health announced changes in the family allowances. While that is all to the good, while it may be a forerunner of something more substantial, it is only a sop at the very outside to the great income group that is forgotten in this budget, and a belated one at that. However, it does give us hope that a new view has been taken by the minister and the administration that the budget is not immutable and unchangeable when it is brought before the house.
Before turning to other considerations, on behalf of the Social Credit group I want to register an unqualified protest against the principle of continuing the sales tax at the manufacturer's level. This protest applies also to the absurd procedure that was outlined in the budget the other night whereby the 25 per cent purchase tax on jewelry and related articles, which had been levied at the retail level, is now being moved back from that level to the manufacturer's level with the rate reduced from 25 per cent to 10 per cent. This procedure is nothing more or less than the converting of an ultimate purchaser's tax into a hidden sales tax. This will tend to establish as a fixture this type of taxation on many more things which Canadians have to buy. Let me assure the minister that my protest in this respect is not at all against the taxing of luxuries; it is simply that by hiding the taxes at the manufacturer's level we are extending the principle of hidden taxes which do push up prices and cause all sorts of difficult problems to arise in our economy.
I know that the minister will say that when these taxes are applied at the retail level every purchaser squawks each time a purchase is made. Doubtless he will have in mind the fact that governments are much more fond of taxes which enable them to pluck the goose painlessly. I sympathize with them, but I trust that when the minister concludes the budget debate he will either yield to the general demand of Canadians with respect to the sales tax being removed or have some more satisfactory explanation for retaining it, and its allied excise, processing and turnover taxes, than was outlined in his speech of last Tuesday, from which I should like to quote this small portion:
The public in peacetime will only tolerate a level of income tax that is far short of enough to yield the revenues that Canada requires now and is going to require in years to come.
In other words, the minister says to the poor man with reference to these hidden taxes, "You are too dumb to protest these
The Budget-Mr. Loiv taxes that you cannot see, and therefore you will just have to keep on paying them."
A careful study of the minister's speech reveals some interesting evidence of a departure from the rigid horse-and-cart economic and financial outlook that has been so common with most of his predecessors. I want to congratulate him most heartily on this new attitude, and I do so sincerely. Quite a number of the things that the minister said in his speech indicate that he has been giving some independent study to the very great and pressing problem of how to achieve an economy in which there is optimum production and optimum consumption, the two basic essentials of a strong, happy, united, and peaceful Canada. I think I am right in saying that he must have inclined an ear to some of the principles of the economics of abundance that Social Crediters have been propounding so consistently and so vigorously over the past fifteen years. Here is one evidence, to be found at page 1786 of Hansard:
It seems to me that the time has now come when our objective-
I want you to note that he says the time has now come. Why it had not come before is anybody's guess, but it would indicate that he had not realized that it should come.
-should be to sustain our present high levels of output, avoiding the evils of unemployment on the one hand and further inflation on the other . . . The best opinion I have been able to form leads me to believe that we can hold the current levels if we, and others in like position, act sensibly.
In other words, the minister realizes now that depressions result from wrong policies that have been made and followed by men. He thinks that there need not be a depression if we act sensibly. We agree with him one hundred per cent, but we believe that the minister will have to go much further yet and declare that, as long as he has direction of financial policy, he will use it and see to it that all forms of taxation and other restrictions that discourage and hold down the level of production of wanted goods and services will be removed; and secondly, that he will see to it that the supply of mass consumer purchasing power is maintained at a level that will ensure optimum consumption of the materials and services that we do produce. If he does those things, he will be acting sensibly. Moreover, he will be discharging the responsibilities of his high office as no other minister of finance in Canada ever has.
Again, on page 1789 of Hansard, column 2, the hon. gentleman is reported as saying:
In some cases, we can observe the occasional emergence of surpluses and of bargain sales by retailers, something which we had almost forgotten to be a normal part of business at certain seasons of the year.

speechtext:
In rising to give my impressions of this budget, Mr. Speaker, may I say that some of the things I have heard said about it, by those who agreed and those who did not agree, reminded me of my early training. I came from a country where the people speak good English; in fact, some people think they speak the best English in the world in the city of Dublin. But whether that is true or not, when I came to this country I found it difficult to understand certain expressions of speech. Amongst the men in the boarding houses I heard expressions like "he's crazy"; "that makes me mad"; "I guess"; and "you bet"-and when the man did that, I did not see any stakes. When a man was said to be crazy, I did not see him looking any different from anybody else; and when he was mad, he was smoking his pipe of peace. I found that those were current expressions. I found another expression, namely, the word "some" in the expressions "he's some sport" and "he's some man". When I hear hon. members say that it is a bribery budget, I just take that as an expression of speech.
I do not think that hon. members think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is guilty of bribery. But in the sense in which it is stated, I think I might use the expression of a great teacher: Let him that is without the sin of bribery cast the first stone. Any man who sends out a Hansard or anything he gets free from this government is guilty of bribery in some way.
The budget was said to be a political budget, and it is. It is a dandy. But it is doing nothing more than carrying out the wishes and meeting the needs of the people. I have not heard of anyone who wants to

have turned back again the exemptions that were granted to him. It is said to be an election budget, and it is. It is a dandy election budget. I do not know that any other party of any other complexion in this house could have done much better. Then, it is a popular budget because it helps everybody. I do not think there is anyone in Canada who is not exempt in this budget. It is a popular budget because it helps the man with the small income. A Winnipeg paper said that it has popularity written all over it. It was possible because of the courage, foresight and thrift of the past administration. They prepared for it. If the Minister of Finance were here, I would say "thanks" to him, for several reasons. If I did not say "thanks" to him I would lack gratitude and heart.
I sent the minister some telegrams and they meant something. I also sent him a good many letters telling him that I thought that the exemptions of the income tax payers should be raised; that the small businessman should certainly have far more consideration; that the business tax should be reduced; and that the whole range of nuisance taxes should be reduced. Three years ago I stood up in this house and stated that the jeweler's tax was not altogether fair because there were sold by jewelers necessities that should have been exempt even in wartime.
What has happened? When I say "thanks" to the minister I want to be able to prove my reason for doing it. In reply to these telegrams and letters which we and many others sent, we find that thirty-two per cent of the taxpayers, totaling 750,000, have been exempted altogether from tax-paying. Therefore we have a right to say "thanks". The next largest cut in taxation is with regard to soft drinks; $24-5 million has been lopped off the soft drinks. I am sure the boys and girls and some men and women all over Canada will say "thanks" to the minister. Those who pay for their sleepers will say "thanks" because of the reduction in the taxation on transportation, which is S17 - 9 million. The taxes of those who bite on a candy bar have been reduced by $16-6 million. Those of us all over Canada who have a sweet tooth say "thanks" to the minister. No doubt it is a popular budget. I wonder how the imagination of the opposition can carry them along to find many defects in this budget. I can admire them in their ingenuity and in their ability to twist the English language to suit their needs if they can make it anything other than a popular budget.
There are three things about this budget that stand out and that appeal to me. First, it will help to maintain a high level of employment-this is quite evident-and pros-

perity will continue. We have the word of the minister himself that prosperity will continue.

speechtext:
Anybody who thinks differently has not as good an imagination as I have.
The minister has prophesied before. We judge a man by what he does, by what he says and by what he produces. His former prophecies have been fairly close to the mark. The second thing that this budget shows is that trade is a basis for prosperity. It pledges the government to a maximum of trade with the whole world. It wants Canadians to buy more from the United Kingdom and to sell more to the United States. To any man who does not see logic in that policy, I say there is something fallacious about his thinking. It did show the reasonableness and the necessity of high taxation in a time of economic boom. That is the time for people to pay taxes and pay off their wartime debt. Last year the minister showed good sense in keeping money where it would help to reduce taxation and keep down inflation. Everybody knows, as I do, that picture shows and entertainment places of all descriptions have sprung up in different cities throughout Canada. Why? Because it paid; because working people had money to spend. Why is it that so much money is spent in Canada on the beer business? Because people have money in their pockets to spend. Therefore was it not quite reasonable for the minister to take off a slice of this money and help to pay off the war debt? I think high taxation is most commendable in prosperous times. Just think, $1 billion-I cannot imagine a billion of money. I know what twenty-five cents and $100 are; but when it gets up to a million it is hard for me to understand. I never saw a million in one place in my life. When it comes to one billion I just cannot comprehend it. The sum of $1,600 million war debt has been paid off since the war. That reduction took place since the wartime peak in taxation. The reduction in taxation amounted to $1,300 million. That is a wonderful feat to take place during the time when Canada was being changed over from war to peace industry, when men in the forces and men engaged in war work had to be transferred into peacetime industry. It is an outstanding
The Budget-Mr. Mclvor feat of the government and it is certainly commendable. I shall use the first slang word I used after coming to this country. It is certainly "some" budget.
I have two or three suggestions to make to the minister for his next budget. First, the mining industry of northern Ontario needs some consideration. Whether it should come in the form of a reduction in taxation or from a rise in the price of gold, I do not know. I leave that to the ingenuity of the Minister of Finance and the other ministers with him, which includes the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), because he knows what is needed.
I make this suggestion because I remember the depression-and this is one of the reasons why I consented at one time to a group of enthusiasts allowing my name to go before a convention. I did that because of the dastardly-I should not use that word-because of the depression. I went out into the country thirty-five miles and had a dinner of boiled wheat with no sugar on it and very little milk. The mother of the home was ill. During the depression the mines in northern Ontario-and the hon. member who will follow me knows that very well-Geraldton and Long Lac, and the mines north and northeast of Port Arthur, employed many men from both Port Arthur and Fort William and paid them good wages. Mining in northern Ontario has earned some consideration from the minister and they should get it before he brings down his next budget.
I would suggest to him how he can spend a little more. Tell the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that he must raise the old age pension rate. I promised that I would give expression to the resolution passed by a group of old ^ge pensioners -and there were not many of them as well dressed as I am, and I am not very particular about my clothes. I have said in the house, Mr. Speaker, that if the Liberal party were left in power long enough the old age pensioners-

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is
always a pleasure to listen to our genial friend, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I know that he speaks with sincerity, but I shall not discuss the soundness of some of his references to the budget. I realize, as he does, that on any occasion a budget is a very important document. It has grown in importance as the years have gohe by. I have listened to many budgets in this house, Mr. Speaker, as you have; and the budget today is probably of greater importance than ever before. It concerns the lives of our people more than ever before. With centralization of government, and all that is involved today in the administration of our national affairs, the budget has grown to be of even greater importance than it has been in years gone by.
I quite appreciate, as you do, sir, that in the discussion of the budget we are expected to discuss the government's fiscal policies or lack of policies. We understand what is indicated by the budget, what we might expect from it. We realize it involves many matters which are controversial from a poli-

tical point of view, having regard to whatever political attitude one may have to the conduct of our affairs.
However, before I proceed to set out some of those features in the budget which appear to me to be unique changes from those policies which I have always understood the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, to follow, may I place before the house an issue which I feel is not one of political controversy.
After all, we saw within the past week that as a House of Commons we have been able to deal with matters with a great degree of unanimity when a common purpose, such as the great purpose of peace, is involved. We will recall the almost complete unanimity indicated in the house when the Atlantic pact was under discussion.
The issue to which I shall now refer, second only in importance to the Atlantic pact at this time, is the forthcoming conference of prime ministers of the British commonwealth to be held in London durfng the Easter recess. It does seem to me that when we realize the situation in the world today, and when we realize that the trade within that commonwealth is rapidly slipping away from us, we must recognize that these issues are of vital concern to every thoughtful Canadian.
I observe that the London Daily Telegraph states editorially that it hopes the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. St. Laurent) will be at the commonwealth prime ministers' conference in April. It states that his presence would make for the authoritativeness and completeness of those discussions. I quote:
Nevertheless it is hoped he will be able to make the journey. The subjects to be reviewed are of supreme importance and his presence would make authoritativeness of their discussions complete.
It goes on to say:
No one can foretell how the grandsons of the members of the coming conference will feel about their common interests and connections; nothing should be done that will hamper them in adapting institutions to their own ideas.
Mr. Bevin is reported only yesterday in the Daily Telegraph to have said that it was of vital importance to the whole of the commonwealth of nations that the prime ministers should be present at that conference, not only because of the danger threatening the western world, but because, so far as the commonwealth is concerned, of equal importance is the falling off of trade and the changing attitude of the United Kingdom government toward trade with Canada particularly.
May I suggest that, after all, Canada is the senior and the greatest dominion, the largest partner in the commonwealth. Let me take this opportunity to urge upon the Prime Minister, in view of this press report, the necessity of his attending the conference. I notice

that the Prime Minister has stated through the press that if necessary he would attend in person. It is further stated, however, that if he felt it unnecessary he would send the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). I feel that in keeping with the national dignity of Canada, in keeping with the importance of this situation, when every other commonwealth nation is being represented by its prime minister, the Prime Minister of Canada should be there.
Then, there are several other important reasons. There is the matter of our future trade relations with the United Kingdom and other sections of the empire. The prime ministers of those other commonwealth countries will be there. The rapid and continuing deterioration of our trade is alarming everyone today who has paused to think of what may happen in the future.
We can see a possible economic crisis in Canada, especially in connection with agricultural marketing, unless those markets, today being lost so rapidly, are recovered for us. I urge that the Prime Minister consider seriously before he sends any new member of his cabinet, no matter how bright he may have been in other fields of activity, to represent this country. He would be the only deputy attending, and would be representing the largest dominion and the one most concerned.
During the past ten years we have negotiated for primary products over one hundred and twenty-four contracts with the United Kingdom government. Twenty-two of those were in force at one time. Today, with the exception of our wheat agreement, we have only three. These contracts negotiated with Canada were for periods averaging one or two years. Not only have we lost those contracts, but we have failed to fulfil some of them, and they have been curtailed accordingly-to a point which, I am sure, must concern ministers in the government, if they pause to realize what is happening.
Everyone in this country is concerned with what this may do to the agricultural economy of Canada. That crisis will materialize just as surely as night follows day if this government fails to rouse itself to a realization of the situation which is falling about them, and which they seem to accept so complacently at this time in a hush-hush fashion before election time, apparently wishing to say nothing about it.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) went over to Great Britain last December, I believe it was, to see what he could do about the situation. He came back with less than he took with him. It is apparent that there is no use sending the Minister of Agriculture, because the result of his last trip indicates
The Budget-Mr. Rowe that the more trips he makes the fewer markets he gets for Canada.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is certainly no more fitted to represent the primary industry of Canada than is the Minister of Agriculture. At least the Minister of Agriculture is politically astute, even if he has not shown much business capacity in dealing with this problem in Great Britain.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I got all I asked for.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
You did not ask for enough, then. That is proof that the minister is not a good trader. I know he is a good politician; but I have no confidence in his business ability, so far as selling our agricultural production is concerned.
And, bearing in mind the vote of want of confidence we have before us, I am not so sure that I have any greater confidence in any of the other gentlemen on the front benches than I have in the Minister of Agriculture-and that is at least some slight compliment to him.
The fact of the matter is that the United Kingdom has turned and continues to turn away from Canada, so far as buying these products is concerned. She is buying her stores of food products from other countries -products which formerly she bought from us. The United Kingdom is, as hon. members must know, one of the most stable markets for agricultural products this country has had since confederation.
Let me repeat that while at one time we had twenty-two contracts with the United Kingdom for the supply of agricultural products, we have only three at this time, with the exception of our wheat contract. Yet Great Britain has made over forty contracts with foreign countries, some of which are behind the iron curtain. She has made contracts with Russia; she has made contracts with Poland; she has made contracts with Holland and with Denmark, and with many other countries. She has traded materials in a wholesale national bulk barter deal on a long-time basis. She has exchanged steel and coal and precision tools and heavy factory equipment that we needed in Canada during the past two or three years. Anyone who knows anything about business realizes that these markets are slipping away from us.
There has never been a conference of commonwealth prime ministers as important for the future life of the primary producer in Canada as the one to be held in London during the Easter holidays. Yet the Prime Minister is not going to attend. Perhaps this is another emergency. Every time they want to get some fictitious bill through parliament

The Budget-Mr. Rowe we are told there is another emergency. Perhaps the Prime Minister will tell us what the emergency is that he cannot attend this conference. I hope that the future welfare of the great agricultural industry of this dominion, and of our primary producers and industrial people who are looking for increased trade with Great Britain, does not depend upon one of the junior members of the government. When such an experienced hand as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has failed, why send a boy to do a man's job?
It has been stated that there is a dollar shortage, but it has also been stated that by 1952 Great Britain does not expect to have a dollar shortage. Yet she has made ten-year agreements with these other countries. I take second place to no one in this house in my allegiance to the British commonwealth of nations. My people came from Great Britain and I have every regard for that country. As was said yesterday, it gives me a thrill to hear "O Canada" sung, but it gives me a greater thrill to hear "God Save the King." I love the British empire and-I think every hon. member has the same feelings- I am proud that I am a British subject. But with all respect to the mother country, I say that the hour has come when we should know what her policy is going to be. We should know whether these lines of sentiment that have been binding us to her are still holding. We should know whether she is going off on a new state-planned socialist trend. We should know whether or not she is going to help us in the sale of our products. Before you took the chair, Mr. Speaker, you were one of the old-time Liberals who believed in the Liberal policies of long ago. Now in the twilight of your political career it certainly must mean something to you to see the way ;he government is drifting toward the socialization of our lives.
We are seeing a political courtship. We have heard how the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has already received his income tax return from this government. I have been here longer than my socialist friends and 1 want to warn them about the groom they are flirting with at the present time. I remember seeing in that same corner some years ago members of the western Progressive party but they were absorbed entirely by the party to your right. You will remember those days, Mr. Speaker. The members of the government have divorced themselves from their old principles. They want to follow on in the way they are going with the blueprint and fashion plate of the socialist party before them.
When the wedding day will be, heaven only knows. Will it be in June or October?

I notice from the British papers it is rumoured that the government has moved up the election date by three months in order to deal with the conclusions of this all-important conference of British commonwealth prime ministers. In London they consider that that is important enough to warrant the presence of all the prime ministers, but here in Canada the government say that they will just send one of their boys over to represent this country. Now that they have moved the election up three months I would like to know when they intended to have it before it was moved up. However, that is a top secret that will likely be known by the Grits in London before it is known by the Tories in Canada.
I suggest to the Prime Minister in all sincerity that there is a necessity for his attending this conference. It is vital so far as our security from a military point of view is concerned. Never in the history of this country have our markets been more seriously threatened. The British papers have said that the Prime Minister can speak with greater authority than anyone else in representing us. I urge upon him that he should find out if it is the policy of the British government to continue to negotiate long-term trade contracts for products which were supplied until recently by Canada.
We are part of the British commonwealth of nations, by sentiment it is true, but we have also built up a great trade through the empire trade agreements. Now they propose to pay more money to countries in the sterling area and ignore us. Not only are they making contracts for two years; they are making them for ten years. They are casting the die for the future. Why is this divorce occurring?
The government has been trying to mimic the socialist government of Britain in their state planning. But they seem to be breaking away from them because they figure that the conference of British commonwealth prime ministers is not so important. They do not seem to figure that this trade is most important. They have been carrying on a type of policy such that no one knows where they are going. I believe that Britain could well be asked to tell us what we can hope for in the future.
As I have said, contracts have been made with Poland, Russia, Hungary and other iron curtain countries, as well as other countries outside the iron curtain. The prime ministers of other commonwealth countries evidently have been asked by Britain to purchase as much as they can in the sterling bloc. In other words, they have been almost told by Britain to purchase in the sterling bloc. Are we to be placed on the Indian list so far as empire trade is concerned? These are mat-

ters that concern the life and hopes of every young man who is starting in business in Canada. What is the emergency? What is the trouble?
Those are things the Prime Minister of Canada should want to know because I assure him that the people of this country want to know. They want to know what is happening. Great Britain is to lend Russia $36 million which will be spent to purchase non-military supplies in the United Kingdom. These heavy materials are to go behind the iron curtain. I know I am on dangerous ground when I criticize the policies of another country, but I think it is important to bring to the attention of the Prime Minister any policy that affects the life of this country.
I think if I were in the Prime Minister's place I would not send anyone else over there to represent me. I would go myself and ask the Prime Minister of Great Britain, the Prime Minister of Australia, the Prime Minister of New Zealand, and every prime minister there, what this is all about. I would ask them if they have formed a bloc against Canada. I am not going to blame the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for everything. He made a poor deal. I have made some poor deals in my life, but I never made as bad a one as he did. If I had I would have gone broke, and everybody associated with me would have been broken.
This is a trend, Mr. Speaker. The Prime Minister went to Washington. If he can go to Washington why can he not go to London? After all, I think the Prime Minister is a busy man, and I know it is only because he has other appointments and other business to attend to that he has been forced to leave the house at this particular time. If I were Prime Minister I am not sure that I would spend all my time listening to him, or any other member who might be with him on the front benches over here. Therefore I realize that it is only a coincidence that he has left the house at this point. He will likely be back.
I am glad that the Prime Minister was able to take time enough from the discharge of his heavy responsibilities to be in the house to listen to me urging him to attend this important conference. I say in all seriousness that I hope he will attend.

speechtext:
I think he is on his
way now.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I do not need to enlarge on what has happened in the British market. On another occasion I have mentioned that to the house. Hon. members, especially in this particular section of the house, have stressed upon the Minister of Agriculture the dangers that lie immedi-
The Budget-Mr. Rowe ately ahead for agriculture, and I am not going to enlarge on them at the present time.
I should like to deal briefly with some of the issues that might be considered even more controversial. My friend, the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), is quite correct. I am glad that there is one clergyman on the other side of the house who seems able, when he is on his feet, to tell the truth with more clarity than many of the other speakers. I have always appreciated the hon. member for Fort William, and when he said tonight that it was a dandy election budget I think the people of Canada will agree that it was.
I remember being in this house in 1940, and on June 24 of that year I heard a budget speech delivered. I am wondering on what grounds the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, is going to appeal to the country, probably three months before they intended to do so. They have had cyclical budgeting. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) can hardly say the word "cyclical" himself, and he does not understand it after he has said it, because he changes it from day to day. We have had all sorts of signs of change and change and change from those who sit to your right, Mr. Speaker. I have here the remarks that were made by the Minister of Finance in 1940. I shall quote them exactly, because while it is bad enough to misquote a man who is in the house, it would be worse to misquote one who cannot be here. In 1940 our good friend, the late Hon. Mr. Ralston, said:
We realize that increases in indirect taxes disguise the burdens imposed by the war, but they are much more likely to distribute these burdens harshly and unfairly.
We have seen reductions in taxation, and the reductions in taxation have been emphasized. Some people have called it a sunshine budget; others call it a sundown budget. I think it will be sunset as far as the government is concerned. We were told by the Minister of Finance the other night that the taxpayer is going to be saved $369 million in a full year. Even though the year is not quite up he is going to make it as attractive as he can, especially if an election is going to be held soon, and we are told that there will be a saving of $323 million anyway. Yet at the same time we are taking from the taxpayers in sales tax alone over $390 million directly, and no one knows how much it costs the consumer indirectly. The sales tax is probably the most vicious type of indirect taxation.
In the budget speech of 1941 Mr. Ilsley had this to say:
As my colleague said when discussing the increases in personal income taxes which he proposed
2206	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Rowe
in the budget of June, 1940, this is the tax which in principle most approximates ability to pay. We realize that increases in indirect taxes disguise the burdens imposed by the war, but they are much more likely to distribute these burdens harshly and unfairly.
There, Mr. Speaker, we have two former ministers of finance who saw the dangers of indirect taxes, that they would be distributed harshly and unfairly. In another case Mr. Ilsley said that this type of tax was easy to collect. I believe he said "very collectable and very productive", but I remember his saying that it was not the type of instrument that he wished to use because it was taking from the people something they did not understand they were losing. He emphasized that this tax, while comparatively easy of administration and collection, and extremely productive, had marked defects as a fiscal instrument.
This is the point I wish to make, Mr. Speaker: What is the fiscal policy of the party to your right? Somebody says that they have none. They used to have one. Years ago when I first came to the house they claimed to have one. When Sir Wilfrid Laurier led them they claimed to have one. Now there is a new era of state planners taking control, and they seem to have lost their fiscal policy, or have changed it according to the election year.
Last year the Minister of Finance said practically the same thing with reference to indirect taxation. I can well remember that, when our party put on a two per cent sales tax, the ex-Prime Minister almost wept. He said that they certainly would remove it or change it. They changed it as soon as they came into power by putting it up to six per cent, and then later on to eight per cent. Then they said it would have to be kept on because of the war. The war has been over now for four years, and it is still on.
If indirect taxation was so harsh and unfair in those years, what is the result now? In 1940, when the Hon. Mr. Ralston said that indirect taxation was harsh and unfair the total revenue from taxes in Canada amounted to $468,271,000. Now the indirect taxes of this dominion amount to $1,072,360,000. If the extraction of $468 million from the people in total tax revenue was harsh, cruel and unfair, now, just before an election, the extraction of $1,072,360,000 in indirect taxes alone is not very kind to the electors who are being fooled by this budget, if anybody is. It is quite apparent from these figures, Mr. Speaker, that the two previous ministers of finance realized that these indirect taxes simply disguised the burden and distributed it more harshly and unfairly; but that seems to have been completely ignored by the present government.


Last year the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said we had reasonably good prosperity but that we could not lower taxes because if we did so the people would have so much money to spend that the cost of living would go up. With the tendency toward centralization and state bureaucratic planning it is not strange how quickly men come to believe that they can handle someone else's money better than that person can handle it himself. Surely the time has come when the Minister of Finance does not need to tell the farmer on the back concession that he cannot judge whether he needs a new roof on his driving shed, or a new henhouse. Surely the time has come when he and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe)-who is a little better than either of the other two in controlling the lives of the people of Canada-should get together and decide that they can trust the people with their own money. But, they say, ''We can handle it better, because we are handling more of it." This has gone on and on; it has pyramided, until now we take from the people of this country $2,441,650,000 in a year, though I can well remember that when I first came to this parliament the yearly revenue of the government was about $340 million.
I do urge the government to stop, look and listen and mend the error of their ways, as far as extravagance go.es. How can they hope to persuade the people not to be extravagant when today they are taking from those same people more than they ever took in the past; when they have taken $1,600 million more than was required to run the country during the last four years; when the cost of government is higher than in any other peacetime period in our history; when we have more civil servants than we ever had before. I see some of those civil servants in the galleries this evening.	We have some
very fine civil servants, but it is hard to distinguish them because there are so many working for the government now. They are almost falling over each other in some departments. We are adding bureaucrats every year, imposing a colossal burden upon the country.
We were all glad to hear from the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) this evening. He is a kindly gentleman; but whenever he rises we know the government is a bit worried, because he can always be depended upon to stand by them, even when the going is tough. It is true that in this budget, just before an election, the government is handing some of the money back to the people. It is true that there has been a change in policy. Last year the Minister of Finance said he

would not reduce taxes because we were enjoying so much prosperity. This year he says we have even greater prosperity and that he believes this prosperity will continue; yet this year he reduces taxes. I would join with the hon. member for Fort William in his belief that this was certainly intended to be a dandy election budget.
Now I urge the government to take cognizance of what is going on as far as trade and as far as taxes are concerned. Only an election year could bring about these drastic changes. In 1940 the sales tax brought in $140 million; today the government takes about $260 million more from the people of Canada in sales tax than it took in 1940, and at that time they called it a vicious principle.
I urge the government to consider our position in reference to trade and the distance we have gone in state planning, what you might call socialized agriculture. It all fits in with the wide swing to the left, the courtship to which I have referred; and if hon. gentlemen who sit to my left would swing a little to the right I think the marriage could be consummated in the not too distant future. In the interval the Minister of Agriculture and his state planners are riding on a cushion of $324 million of ERP money, of which $216 million was earmarked for the purchase of agricultural products in Canada, together with $235 million loaned by this country for the purchase of agricultural products. If at a time when we have this amount of money to spend we cannot save our markets, what are we going to do later on, when we have no such assistance? Not only will the farmers have their cellars full of potatoes they cannot sell; not only will the canning factories be loaded up with raspberry jam, as they are now; but you will be tearing out apple trees in various districts because you cannot sell the apples. If the United States declares wheat a surplus product, what are we going to do with our wheat? Are we trying to copy the British planning; or is that planning the reason the British markets are slipping away from us? Where are we going to sell these products? This country never needed leadership and stability as much as it does now. It never before so badly needed a man with enough courage to turn back to the right and talk realities and tell the people the truth, even at election time. You do not get very much for nothing in this world.
I believe my time has almost expired, Mr. Speaker, so I must conclude shortly. In the United Kingdom we have seen the spectacle I have referred to. I repeat that I take second place to no one in my admiration for Britain and the gallant battle she has carried on in the last few years. I take second place to no one in my admiration of her leadership
The Budget-Mr. Rowe in the industrial life of the world, which continued for almost a hundred years. But her first mistake was made even before the first war, when the famous Asquith socialism was brought into operation. At that time Britain began to lose her grip on the industrial leadership of the world. So it was not only the two great wars through which she passed that brought her to her present position; the socialist doctrines that have been followed have played an important part. If that is not true, with all the state planning, the national socialism, the nationalization of this and that industry, why is it that everybody is working yet everybody is rationed? Look at this great continent of North America: look at this country of ours. The Minister of Agriculture and others paved the way in western Canada many years ago; and they did not do it by asking for sops from the government, though the minister has thrown out a good many since. It was not done that way, and no one knows it in his heart of hearts better than the minister. Now, whether the election is in June or October, he knows he has lost the confidence of the people of this country, and hopes and prays to God that he may be saved from the avalanche and the debacle we will have to clean up when we form the next government. Why is it, Mr. Speaker, that today 41-7 per cent of the entire national income of the United Kingdom is taken in taxes, in order to kid the people that it is being handed back to them in various ways?

speechtext: Tell us about the British by-elections.

speechtext:
My hon. friend is back on the question of an election. Let me tell him that in the United States, where the standard of living is twice as high, they take only 26 per cent of the national income in taxation; while in Sweden, a model in many respects, they take only about 18 per cent. So I urge the government not to be influenced by the gibes of those to my left. It is better to go down to defeat alone than to carry socialism further and go down to defeat with a partner more socialist than you are. To my hon. friend who has interrupted me I say he must be a great admirer of the Right Hon. Herbert Morrison. But on September 5, 1945, Mr. Morrison-who maybe is not as socialisti-cally inclined as you are but leans toward that dangerous path that you have been following-said this: "We've left behind the scarcity economics of a capitalist world." What did he say in January, 1949, only four years later? What a difference just a few years make! Indeed, in this government what a difference just a few months make! In January, 1949, Mr. Morrison says: "Don't promise the moon unless you are able to deliver the goods, and it is pretty doubtful

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny if you can." That is why I am going to vote for the amendment expressing want of confidence in this government, feeling sure myself that the people of Canada have lost confidence in this government and are looking for the type of leadership and stability that has been so emphatically, eloquently and clearly displayed by the greatest leader in this house, the leader of the party to which I have the honour to belong.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I cannot hope, Mr. Speaker, to emulate the hon. member who has preceded me in the eloquence that he has displayed. I always admire the facility with which he can speak in such a rapid-fire fashion. In his time he must have been a wonderful auctioneer. If he was not one, he would have been a good one, particularly if he had something to sell.
The hon. member made a few references to the party to which I have the honour to belong, and warned the government or the Liberal party that they were going down the road to socialism. He also issued a warning to this party, for which we are duly thankful, that we may be swallowed up by the Liberal party, as was the Progressive party at an earlier date.

speechtext: Do you not think you will be?

If you will listen you will hear them. In the past the party advocated an increase in the sales tax. In case it might be thought that the hon. member for Rosedale was speaking only for himself, and was not in a responsible position, which would indicate that he was making an irresponsible speech in this house, may I refer hon. members to the history of the sales tax itself. In 1931 the sales tax stood at one per cent. In that year the Conservative party-it was not progressive officially at that time-the Bennett administration raised it 400 per cent. They made it 4 per cent. Perhaps it was Mr. Bennett's personal idea, I do not know. Perhaps he was not doing it for the party. Perhaps it was just a funny notion that he had, but in 1932 we find that he got the same notion over again and raised it 50 per cent, making it instead of 4 per cent, 6 per cent. Then the Liberals took over. The Liberals took over in 1935 and on the second day of May the following year they raised it to 8 per cent and that is where it has remained until this day. There is the whole history of the sales tax and the action of the various parties on it.
In reading or listening to the present budget one can hardly escape the impression that once again more than half of the Canadian people have been almost completely


disregarded. It is easy enough for the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), or any other hon. member on the government side, to rise in his place and say it is a dandy budget, it is a fine election budget. We all know that; but it is again left to this party to speak for more than 50 per cent of the Canadian people who are not within the income tax brackets at all, and whose situation today is worse than it was a year ago because the cost of living has gone up. To them the thing that stands out the largest in the whole budget is not the action taken to cut income tax rates or to raise exemption levels, because they were not paying income tax anyway, but the fact that the subsidy of forty-six and a half cents a bushel on wheat going into flour has been removed, which means another increase in the price of bread.
There are many people in Canada who already are finding it pretty hard to make ends meet with the prices of bread, milk and other commodities as they are today. It is not only unfair to the consumer but it is unfair to the producer, because the farmers of this country are going to find it difficult in years to come-and this difficulty is now making itself felt-to dispose of their products. If the government is to take action which will raise the domestic price of these products to the consumer, it means that they will sell that much less of their products. Of course there are those who do not believe in subsidizing. In one of his speeches not so very long ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) himself said that he would not be a member of a government which would subsidize housing. That would seem to indicate that he looks the same way on subsidies on food products as well.
I may say frankly to the government that if they accept the philosophy that all subsidies should be removed, then they are going to have to make many changes in all the statutes of this country, because our whole tariff system is based on subsidies. Much of our industry today operates on a subsidy basis. If they are going to extend subsidies to the steel interests, to the gold mining interests, and put up tariff walls to protect the manufacturing industries, they cannot stop there and say that they will remove the subsidies on food products, because that is grossly unfair to the primary producers of Canada.
A criticism has been made of this budget, and I think rightly so-although I am not inclined to use the strong language that was used today in calling it a "bribery" budget- that it was designed to influence the voters at the next election. We had an admission of that from one of the Liberal members this evening who spoke very frankly.
