speechtext:
We have had other instances in the past of political parties attempting to influence voters. Earlier in this session I referred to an article written by the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power), one of the finest members of the house, who spoke out very frankly and admitted that in the past both the Liberals and the Conservatives have bought votes with cash on the barrelhead. Whatever may be said about that system itself, at least it is an honest system. You pay the cash and you get the vote, maybe. Some of the experiences have been that they were not always sure of the votes they bought, and that in itself had a tendency to hold them back from spending too much money. But now the government has struck with a "new look" in politics. Instead of spending party funds, all they need to do is to squeeze the taxpayers for two or three years and in an election year give some of it back to the voters and say, "what fine fellows we are." I am sure that the people of Canada, the taxpayers of this country, are not going to look kindly upon that kind of tactics. They expect from the people in public life a certain amount of frankness. If the Liberal party feel that they have done the proper thing in the last few years, let them place their record before the people and let them be judged by that record. To attempt to influence the voter by giving him something which was taken away from him, and making it appear as if he were receiving a present, does not speak well for the high level to which politics in this country should aspire.
I come now to agriculture. It can be fairly said that this budget leaves the farmers out in the cold. About all that happens is that those farmers who did pay income tax of substantial sums may be relieved of part of the burden. But that was not the most serious feature of taxation, nor the thing that the farmers objected to most. What the farmers have been objecting to most for a long period of years is the cost of production of the things which they have to produce. This year, that is worrying the farmers more than it has been for a long time, because the prospects are that the price of farm produce is going to come down. When he arrived back from England the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) spoke to the organized farmers of Canada and warned them that the prospects are they must expect less money for their grain, their livestock and all their other products. We have only to look at the price of butter to see where the trend is leading at the present time. Farmers know that it is a two-sided question. The farmers of 29087-140
The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny Canada have always been very fair in approaching the question of prices and markets. They have never asked for all that the market could bear. There were opportunities for farm prices to rise to much greater heights than they did, had that been permitted by price ceilings, but the organized farmers and individual farmers in this country never pressed the government to allow the prices of farm produce to go beyond reasonable levels.
What the farmer wants most is stability. He is not asking for an opportunity to profiteer from his fellow man. He asks only for the opportunity to earn an honest living and to receive full remuneration for his labour. That is why the cost of production to farmers is just as important as, and in the next few years will be more important than, the prices of the produce they sell. The farmer realizes that the price he receives for the surplus products to be exported will be largely governed by the conditions in those markets to which they are shipped. And the only way in which he can receive better prices than those markets command would be through government subsidies. That being so, farmers realize that the only way they can remain solvent and in production is to keep costs of production down to a reasonable level, in order to produce at a reasonable price.
At the convention held last summer by the Liberal party the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) made a speech. Resolutions were passed-I have copies of them. I have looked through those resolutions carefully, and I find that the two things they did promise in definite terms to the farmers of Canada were that the cost of production would be reduced by government action, and that stable markets would be found for surplus production for the next several years.
Let me say that those are just the things the farmers are wondering about. What has been the result? Has the government taken action to review the cost of production? One has only to ask what happened in connection with freight rates. They went up 21 per cent; and hardly had that been done when the railways applied for another increase of 20 per cent, which is now being considered. If that is allowed, the farmers will pay 41 per cent more in freight rates than they did a year ago.
Certainly that is not going to reduce the cost of production either for the western farmers or for those in the east. Then, what about the price of farm implements? All those things enter into the cost of production. Yet, from year to year, since the ceilings have been taken off, the farmers have seen those costs climb. Today, when we have reached a point where the prices of farm products are

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny almost sure to come down, those costs of production are either rising or remaining stationary. This government has not redeemed its pledge to the farmers to reduce those production costs. Neither have they redeemed their pledge to find suitable markets for the surplus products offered by the farmers of Canada. We in the C.C.F. party suggested to the governments some time ago that in order to look after surplus production both of prairie farmers and farmers producing apples, livestock and other products, the government should be prepared to assist in making bilateral trade agreements with various countries which would be prepared to exchange their products for the primary products of Canada.
Replying to that in his budget the Minister of Finance said the government was absolutely opposed to any such arrangement, and used this as an excuse for not doing it.
The third practical objection to this line of approach is one in which most, but not all, members of this house will agree. It is that the application of a policy of barter, bilateral deals, and discrimination requires widespread governmental control of private trade, and even the extension of trade by agencies of the government itself.
Let me pause there to ask the minister what is wrong with the government's becoming an agency for trade in disposing of our primary products? Is that not what the wheat board is constituted to do at the present time? If the philosophy of the Minister of Finance were followed to its logical conclusion it would mean that we would have no wheat board in Canada. Because if the minister is opposed to the government's becoming an agency for buying or selling primary products, then he is of course opposed to the wheat board's handling of grain.
Then at a later point the minister said in his budget speech:
It is apt to lead to more government buying and selling, frequently involving subsidies and trading losses.
Let me say to the minister that, if he thinks a government can save money by avoiding subsidies at certain times in the marketing of primary products in this country, he will find that if another major depression comes- and it will come if the farmers of this country cannot dispose of their products-it will cost the government far more in the form of relief, and bring far less benefits to all concerned than a few well-placed subsidies.
So much for agriculture. There are other very serious omissions from the budget to which I wish to refer at this time. People have been led to believe that this year the government was going to announce an overall social security program which would provide greater benefits for those receiving old age pensions, provide assistance for those

who are crippled or disabled, and also provide a general national health plan. We in this group have been waiting impatiently for some such action on the part of the government, to show that this is going to be done. We felt that perhaps when the budget was brought down the government would reveal its plan in this respect.
Again we have been disappointed. We find there is nothing in the budget to show that provision is being made for an over-all social security program such as was promised as far back as 1945 by the administration, and hinted at every year since that time.
We find also that one of those things which some of us have urged over a period of time has been left out entirely-no mention made of it-and that is some form of financial assistance to the provinces for educational purposes. Let me hasten to say I realize as well as anyone that education, from the standpoint of administration, is in the hands of the provinces. Nor do I wish to raise any controversy about provincial autonomy. But there is nothing in our constitution which would prevent this or any other government in Ottawa making substantial grants in aid to the provinces for the purpose of raising and equalizing educational standards.
In order to put this party's stand on the record so far as that question is concerned, let me quote the resolution passed by the national convention of the C.C.F., held at Winnipeg last summer. We say:
While fully recognizing that education is rightly under provincial jurisdiction, a C.C.F. government, in its first term of office, will collaborate with the provinces to provide and equalize educational opportunities for all Canadian children. It will make every effort to make sufficient funds available to help the province to:
1.	Ensure that the necessary schools and colleges are built and equipped.
2.	Provide, by scholarships and otherwise, financial assistance to deserving students.
3.	Assure teachers an adequate salary.
4.	Assist adult educational programs on a broad scale.
5.	Encourage musical and dramatic art, the arts and crafts, and assist recreational and physical fitness programs.
We feel that that is a reasonable program to expect at this time from the federal government. The other day the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) made an announcement of the government's policy with respect to television-a most important announcement. Let me say that I agree with him; television is important enough to remain as a public utility, on the same basis as the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
This however happens to be a field of education which, to say the least, staggers the imagination. If television were applied in this country for broadening and raising educational standards it would do a great

service not only to this generation but to all future generations. It is the most revolutionary means of communication we have today. The development of television has not been carried out in Canada, but this is a field into which the federal government could enter with great propriety and spend the large sums of money necessary to make television available to the schools of the country. No one will deny that there is no single municipality, school district or even province that could attempt to give that kind of service to the schools because of the great capital expenditures that would be involved. In this connection the federal government could properly enter into the field of education and provide the necessary facilities, both at the broadcasting and receiving ends.
I know that this will sound revolutionary to some hon. members when television is not yet in commercial use, but let us not forget that only a few years ago we did not have jet-propelled planes or atom bombs or many of the things that are realities today. It is not expecting too much to say that it will not be long before television in the United States, which is now on a commercial basis, will be put to social and educational uses. Under a properly controlled public utility setup television can play a great role in the enlightenment of future generations.
Another omission from the budget which I regret is one in connection with a public investment program. This was referred to by the government in 1945 when we were led to believe by the speeches made, particularly by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), that the government was planning to spend large sums of money in the prairie provinces to develop our natural resources and expand our secondary industries. I am disappointed to find that there is no provision in this budget for that kind of work.
Those who know the prairies realize that the farmers are in a precarious position. Given one or two years of drought or some other condition that causes a crop failure and many of the people there find themselves in a bad financial state. One reason is that we do not have sufficient secondary industries or industries of a processing or manufacturing nature to absorb the shock of a crop failure. We are dependent too much upon one type of economy.
On the other side of the scale we find that in eastern Canada there is a large concentration of working people in the cities. During the war there was a great housing shortage and much overcrowding and congestion. On the other hand, we have the wide-open spaces on the prairie, we have the climate and we have everything to make life comfortable.

The Budget-Mr. Zaplitny Those of us who have lived on the prairies for a number of years cannot understand why one would want to live in a city in eastern Canada. However, there may be two sides to that question.
The fact remains that we have an unbalanced economy. There is too great a concentration of people in eastern Canada and there is too great an expanse of space in western Canada. Something should be done about it, not only to relieve congestion in the cities of eastern Canada but to help to develop our great resources and the possibilities that we have on the prairies. When I refer to the prairies I do not want anyone to think that they are just flat, open spaces. The fact is that we have prairie land, we have park land and we have mining districts, such as those in northern Manitoba and northern Saskatchewan. Then there are the oil fields of Alberta and the coal fields. We have in western Canada the possibilities of a great industrial area.
I attended a meeting outside the house at which the Minister of Agriculture spoke and he told the meeting that there was no reason why there should not be 15 million people in the three prairie provinces within a few years. I see no reason either, unless the government is not willing to supply the capital necessary to give an impetus to the development of our natural resources. If that is not done both the Minister of Agriculture and I will be pushing up the daisies for a long time before there are 15 million people on the prairies. There are great possibilities there but they require capital for their development. The federal government could properly go into those areas and develop those industries.
It has been suggested that there should be a steel rolling mill in one of the prairie provinces. Someone will ask whether we have the iron ore there. The fact is that northern Manitoba has ore of all kinds. The ground has hardly been scratched there. speechtext:
I am glad that he has identified himself. Nor do I think it will be necessary for the Prime Minister to invite any other member on the other side of the house. The hon. member for Dufferin-Sim-coe returned many times to that point. He urged the Prime Minister to go to London. He said that Canada should be represented by the Prime Minister, and that the Prime Minister should not send one of his boys over there. The Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) sent one of his boys to say that to the Prime Minister tonight. He did not come here and say that to the Prime Minister.


I was greatly amused in listening to his remarks because so much of them did not concern the budget. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe referred to contracts with the United Kingdom. I do not know if he would prefer to have many more contracts, but I might remind the house of the stand that his party took on the measure sponsored by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) which was passed by the house recently. I understood that they were against the contracts. The hon. member should not grieve over the fact that the Minister of Agriculture has not concluded as many contracts as hon. members opposite desire.
The hon. memher had a lot to say about what he called political speeches. I do not know how I should describe the speech he made tonight. I do not know whether it was a constructive one, if there were any suggestions for the government to put into effect, or if it was merely a speech to raise a fuss and to try to impress some of the voters of the country. I hope that the voters will read his speech, and I rely entirely on their sound judgment to decide as to its merit.
I should like to refer now to the speech delivered by the distinguished member for Muskoka-Ontario on the budget. He was supposed to criticize the budget. I took notes of what he said, and I think one can summarize his argument in this way. He said that it was a very good budget but that it was bad for them because they fear that an election will be held this year. If you will refer to Hansard you will see that on the night the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) delivered his speech on the budget, the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario asked if there were any taxes left. That was an excellent appreciation of the good policy of the government. Continuing this afternoon, it was pretty hard for him in view of the drastic conclusion he had arrived at the other night.
If we want to understand the attitude of the Progressive Conservative party on fiscal policy we must refer to their attitude in the past since the beginning of the last war. I was not in the house before 1945, but I read the newspapers, I referred to Hansard, and I became acquainted with the attitude of my hon. friends. They constantly demanded higher and higher expenditures for war purposes. They made their demands in good faith, and they were probably trying to help the country to win the victory over the enemy as soon as possible. Nevertheless at that time they did their best to contribute towards augmenting the expenditures of the country. They attacked the government because they said at that time the government was too lenient. They said that people

did not enlist quickly enough, and that the government did not spend enough money for munitions and supplies, for grants and loans to other countries, and so on. If the government had followed the suggestions of the hon. members in the official opposition what would have happened? The debt, instead of being over $16 billion at the end of the war, would have been about $20 billion or $25 billion. What would be the attitude of those hon. members today in the face of such a huge debt? Would they ask the government to reduce taxes? The answer is no. They would be obliged to ask the government to maintain high taxes on the people of Canada in order to meet the huge obligations that would be facing this country. That would be the situation of the country and of the government.
At the end of the war the government did the best it could to give fair and just treatment to the veterans, and our veterans charter seemed to be the best in the world. My hon. friends of the opposition did not find that sufficient. Pensions were not high enough; pensions should have been paid not only to veterans but also to those indirectly connected with war occupations. Public works should have been undertaken everywhere.
A few days ago when a motion was before the house to go into committee of supply the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) asked the Minister of Agriculture and the other members of the cabinet to spend hundreds of millions of dollars for a gigantic plan he submitted to the house. Other hon. members rose and submitted demands of the same kind. Now they are saying taxes are too high, that the government should have reduced taxes more and more.
As for controls, at the end of the war and as a consequence of the war there was a great scarcity of certain commodities. The government had to take control of those commodities and distribute them among the people. My friends of the Conservative party fought for the removal of controls. If the government had agreed to their requests then, monopolies would have hoarded the commodities and sold them at prohibitive prices to the more fortunate people, depriving the working people and poorer citizens of this country.
Since the end of the war this government has made a splendid record. It has achieved the tremendous task of consolidating our national debt and reducing it by the tremendous amount of more than $1,500 million. During less than four years the government has demobilized our armed forces, converted our war industries into peacetime industries,
The Budget-Mr. Marquis developed our internal and external trade, given generous pensions to our veterans, contributed to the economic revival of European countries, and established a vast program of social security in Canada. I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) was more than justified in saying that no country in the world can show a better record. If since the beginning of the war this country had been administered by the self-boasting geniuses of the opposition, it seems to me the economic and social situation in Canada would be more comparable to that of the years 1930 to 1935 than that of the years 1945 to 1949.
In his criticism of the budget the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Mac-donnell) referred more to the budget of last year than to the budget of this year. If he wants to examine the records of the two parties he should examine them for the last twenty-five years, let us say. The Liberal party, with its two leaders in thirty years, shows a magnificent record of achievements before the war, during the war and since the war. The Conservative party, which changed its name and is now the Progressive Conservative party, in the same period of time has had half a dozen temporary, acting or not-acting leaders, and in 1935 was ousted from power for lack of clear-sightedness, lack of competence and lack of comprehension of public affairs. This is the straight and brief record of both parties for a quarter century.
But let us come to the criticism put forward by the hon. gentleman. He says this is a bribery budget, but at the same time stresses the fact that the Liberal government has failed in giving married people an exemption of only $2,000. He says his party has promised an exemption of $2,500. Where is the political bribery-in a real, sound reduction, or in a fictitious promise the Conservative party will never make effective? Because they will not be more successful under this new temporary leader than they were under the other, forgotten ones.

I am not easily surprised; I
think the hon. gentleman is more likely to be surprised than I am, but he should be accustomed to that, so his health will not suffer if he is defeated at the next election. If I am not mistaken, he forgot to mention the exemption for children; he forgot to refer to the family and social aspects of this budget. I prefer to see an exemption of $2,000 for a married couple, with an additional exemption of $150 per child, plus the family allowance exempt from taxation for a family of six or eight children under sixteen, than an exemption of $2,500 for childless married people.

The Budget-Mr. Marquis
I thank the hon. gentleman for the following remark. In referring to the budget of the Minister of Finance he said, "This comes to you with the compliments of the Liberal party." He should have said, "with the compliments of the best government we ever had in Canada." He should have added that good and progressive measures always come with the compliments of the Liberal party and the Liberal government. Family allowances have come to this country with the compliments of the Liberal government. The adjustments of family allowances will come this year with the compliments of the Liberal government. Old age pensions have come in this country with the compliments of the Liberal government. The health program has come with the compliments of the Liberal government. More than that, the unemployment insurance plan came to this country with the compliments of the Liberal government. This government may not be perfect, because there is nothing perfect on this earth; but if the hon. member will refer to the political history of Canada for the last twenty or twenty-five years he will see that social measures, good administration, the consolidation and reduction of the debt, always came with the compliments of the Liberal government.
In his remarks the hon. member pointed out that the Minister of Finance was under a disadvantage in not representing a farming constituency, thus insinuating that the present budget does not take care of the farming population. I have the advantage of representing a farming constituency, one in which perhaps nearly all the residents are farmers. There is no city, there is no town. In my constituency there are only parishes composed of farmers and workers. I was born on a farm. When I was young I worked on a farm, and I myself own a farm. I am surprised at the remarks of the hon. gentleman. If there is some group which can criticize this budget, may I say that I do not see how the farmers of my country can criticize a budget which provides exemptions for their average income, exemptions for their large families, and provides at the same time such great social benefits. The government has undertaken to increase the family allowances and to assure stability in prices of farm products.
In raising the exemption to $2,000 for married people and to $150 plus the family allowance without any charge for children under sixteen and to $400 for children over sixteen, it seems to me that this government has given substantial relief to the farmer whose income is not high and who is generally the head of a large family. I have here comparative figures with regard to income taxes which will be levied in 1949 in the United States,

the United Kingdom and Canada. If I may have the consent of the house to do so, I will table these figures.

The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), who can naturally express himself in English far better and far more easily than I can, put on the record a few particularly flashy sentences, and I took note of one of them which was: "Do not promise the moon unless you deliver the goods".
In almost fifteen years, this government has never made large promises. It had to meet the war burden. It had to meet the attack of the opposition when it was fighting this terrible war. It succeeded in maintaining economic stability, order and peace in this country; in preventing subversion and communist attack; it had sent to prison those who were found to be traitors to their country. During that time hon. members of the opposition strongly questioned the attitude of this government and of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) who was then Minister of Justice, because he had some citizens put behind bars and kept in secret pending an investigation which concerned the security of the state. we could never have been able to see that day when Christian democracies are able to send their prime ministers or their representatives to sit around the peace table to discuss the security of our Christian nations, to unite for the benefit of those who want to maintain their faith, their traditions and their creeds, who want to maintain their system of economy and their policies. If the government had not succeeded in arresting those people, perhaps this country would now be in a critical situation.
I referred a few minutes ago to the words of the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) in which he said: "Don't promise the moon, unless you are able to deliver the goods". How often have we recalled in the house all the goods that this government has delivered to the country. We never promised the moon. We never promised what the hon. gentlemen dared to promise at their convention, namely, to give more social security, to give more tax exemptions, to give larger old age pensions, to lower the age limit to sixty or sixty-five and to decrease the taxes in this country. How can a party which did not make an outstanding success of public affairs from 1930 to 1935 perform such a miracle in politics, by giving all that to the people and reducing the taxes in this country? I believe sincerely that these words apply to my hon. friends who promised the moon, but who will never be able to deliver the goods.
I know that my hon. friends of the opposition are gentlemen, and I congratulate them on the efforts they are making to criticize a good administration. I understand that it is an extremely hard thing to do. Mr. Speaker, I regret that the short time at my disposal does not allow me to discuss at very great length the budget now before the house. But if I may make a brief outline of that document, I shall say that the government of this country has made genuine efforts to stabilize our country's economy and reduce our debt considerably. Now that the danger of war is disappearing and that we are beginning a new era, the government is in a position to grant substantial reductions. At the end of the war the taxpayers of this country had to carry a heavy burden. It was difficult for the government to reduce taxes immediately because of the post-war re-establishment which had to be made. There was also the matter of the veterans' pensions. An uncertain period had to be faced.
The Budget-Mr. Marquis
Nevertheless in order to increase the hopes and courage of our people and to allow them to face the post-war period, in 1945 the government reduced taxes by $300 million.
In 1946, as rapidly as demobilization was proceeding, taxes were again reduced by $266 million. By 1947, when demobilization was completed, war industry was practically reconverted to peacetime activity and the government then reduced taxes by $265 million. The year 1948 marked what I might call the end of the war period, but the government felt bound to ask the Canadian taxpayers to accept for one more year pretty heavy taxes, so that it might draw up a plan for the future. However, it still reduced taxes by $92 million. This year the government keeps up its policy of the last few years by granting a tax reduction amounting to $369 million. No election was in the offing in 1945 when the government abolished taxes which were yielding $300 million. An election had just been held, and we had been victorious.
In 1946, there was no talk of elections. With respect to tax reductions, this budget compares favourably with those of 1945, 1946 and 1947. Mr. Speaker, even though at the present time I consider the government's fiscal policy to be a guarantee for the future of this country, I feel that what is more important is the moral well-being of the nation and those principles which must guide the conduct of each and every one of us in public life. I think it is fitting to ask every member here, whatever his political affiliation, not to make a political football of those principles which must direct us, the principles of unity, of love for our country, of faith in our country's capacity to combat subversive doctrines.
I urge my colleagues, should an election be held this year or next year, not to make a political ladder out of the question of communism. Let us not forget that we are entrusted with the responsibility of representing, not only the workers, but all the citizens, all the heads of families, the Christians of this country. To make communism a political weapon is to tear ourselves asunder, to destroy ourselves, to prevent ourselves from reaching our goal. But if we unite to discuss the various political problems, from an economic viewpoint, if we adhere to the leading principles which would make of our nation a Christian nation, faithful, united, well then, Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that the purpose of the North Atlantic pact will be achieved and that Canada will live in peace with the other nations. And should the world revolutionary elements attack us-which God forbid-we shall through courage, strength and the help of God win victory, peace and security.

subtopic: DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I first of all compliment the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon the presentation of his sundown budget of March 22, which he delivered in splendid fashion at that time.
First of all I should like to make mention of the fitting ceremonies which I believe are to take place tomorrow both in Newfoundland and in this capital city, welcoming Newfoundland as the tenth province of this great nation. Tomorrow will be the first day of April, and also the first day in the history of an even greater Canada.
In this connection I should like to read a telegram received yesterday from a gentleman of the cloth in my constituency. This telegram, dated at Lyleton, states:
Lyleton churches, schools, women's institutes, etc. wish you convey to Newfoundland representatives the sincerest good wishes of southwestern Manitoba


trusting increased prosperity for our new sister and for enlarged Canada more influence in promoting world peace. Sunday we sing God Guard Thee Newfoundland, as Newfoundland sings O Canada. If no Newfoundlanders at Ottawa please forward to St. John's.
W. D. Bayley, Minister
That, it seems to me, manifests the spirit among the people of this nation, particularly those from the far-flung prairies, situated so far from the new sister province to become part of this great nation tomorrow. I am sure the ceremonies will be fitting to the occasion, and I add my word of congratulation at this moment.
May I also endorse what was said by my colleague the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) when he spoke in this debate this evening. I, too, think it is most important that our Prime Minister attend the conference of commonwealth prime ministers to be held in Great Britain during the latter part of April. This is even more true when, as has been pointed out during this session, we have lost many markets in the United Kingdom for our agricultural products, and other markets are becoming more precarious every day.
Certainly I am sure every agricultural producer in Canada would wish that the Prime Minister would be able to attend the conference in person so that he might put in his word, and find out what we may expect to happen in connection with future markets for the products of this country, particularly agricultural products. I do not think there was ever a time in our history when it was more important that the Prime Minister should personally attend a conference than that he should delegate one of his ministers, particularly a junior minister.
In presenting his budget the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has certainly demonstrated not only that large tax cuts were possible but that they could have been made progressively in substantial amounts for the last three years without damaging his debt reduction program. Income tax exemptions and various tax reductions were not in the true sense reductions, but were in fact refunds of unnecessary revenues collected from the people in the three years I have mentioned. These reductions were not the result of government savings, as the people realize today. They represent surpluses the government has been collecting over and above its reasonable and justifiable needs. The reductions are made at a time when expenditures are being increased daily. They do not represent any effort on the part of the administration to economize or to return to peacetime efficiency. The public are reasonably charitable towards governments during wartime. They realize that much

must be done in a hurry. However, we have now reached a time almost tour years after the conclusion of the war. This year the Minister of Finance has a surplus of $575 million; last year it was $670 million and the year before $373 million. Thus in three years the federal government through taxation has taken from the public a total of $1,618 million more than it needed.
In 1946-47 the minister should have made tax reductions he is now making, and had he done so he could still have had a surplus of $5 million. In 1947-48 he could have made the reductions he now makes and have had a surplus of $302 million; and in 1948-49 he could have made the tax reductions he now makes and have had a surplus of $203 million.
The funded debt of Canada now stands at a total of $15,600 million, and the debt interest of 1946 was $464 million. In 1947-48 it was $455 million and in 1948-49 it was $463 million. The figure for the last year is of course an estimate. Thus the interest on the debt which we pay this year is $8 million greater than what we paid a year ago.
A year ago the minister made a great deal of the necessity for cyclical budgeting, and at that time went to great lengths to prove just how necessary it was. All that has now been disregarded and thrown to the winds. As was so well said by the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell), it has been clear throughout the last year that this was not an economic cycle at all, but that it was a political cycle, something which is so evident on all sides throughout the country today.
As the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario pointed out, the Minister of Finance was prepared to produce a lemon in 1948 in order to cut a melon in 1949. That was pointed out as likely to happen long months before the budget was presented.
A great majority of the citizens of Canada are not in the income tax brackets. That has already been pointed out in the debate, and the subject was dealt with at considerable length by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Marquis), who has just taken his seat. He pointed out that he is a farmer; he says he was raised on a farm and spent his life there, and that he sees in the budget assistance for the farmers. The hon. member did make reference to the exemptions for both farmers and members of their families. In one respect I would offer my thanks to the government for the announcement made today; because every year since I have been a member in the house hon. members of this party, including myself, have asked for greater consideration in the matter of exemptions for farmers' wives and members of their families who actually performed productive
The Budget-Mr. J. A. Ross work on the farms. In answer to the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) did say today that it is now possible to pay one of the younger members of a family up to $400 for production work, and still show that child as a dependent for exemption purposes.

I happen to have in my file a Free Press which contains headlines on the front page expressing wonder why the delegates to the national Liberal convention held in this city last summer were not allowed to discuss this wheat deal. It never came up on the floor of the convention. I am sure that if it had been the satisfactory deal that some members of the government would like the people of this nation to think it is, it would certainly have been discussed with some gusto at that national gathering of Liberals last summer. No reference was made to it at that time.
This matter affects the prosperity of every individual within Canada, more especially those living in the prairie provinces. I care not what their occupation may be, whether they are school teachers, bankers, garage men, merchants or whatever it may be, either directly or indirectly they are servicing the agricultural industry which produces so much of the essential food for mankind. This is particularly true of the residents of the prairie provinces, no matter what their occupation may be. Therefore most of these people do have a grievance in connection with this matter.
On several occasions during this session the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has discussed the production of rye and he stated that he was the culprit in connection with the handling of it.

I do know something about the production of rye. Ever since I started farming for myself in 1920 I have missed only one year when I did not have some winter rye. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will agree that it does fit into a diversified farming program. I have grown it for early spring and late fall pasture for cattle even though I may not harvest it. But we do generally take the cattle off in May or around the first of June and harvest the crop. The average price from August, 1945, up to February of this year, which is the same as the pooling period for wheat-true enough the price was

up to $4.47-5/8 in 1948-was $2.72 per bushel. That is almost $1 a bushel more than the price of $1.75 for wheat under the pooling arrangement. May I add further that in normal years prior to the outbreak of the war, when all grain was handled on the open market, the usual prevailing price of rye was around 80 per cent or 85 per cent of the prevailing price per bushel of wheat. Year in and year out that was about the approximate comparison, and I think it is rather significant when you compare that with the handling of wheat by the agencies throughout the pooling period. While we are discussing the matter of pools, and more especially for the benefit of my good friends to the left, some of whom are always very antagonistic to the profit system-

May I say that they have also advanced some rather odd ideas about cooperatives in this country. I have before me an article that appeared in the Rural Cooperator under date of February 22 of this year. The article is headed "Consider selves true capitalists". My friends to the left not only argue against profits but they are always arguing against the capitalist system. Therefore I think this article is rather interesting. It reads:
Farmer co-operatives are "off the farm" business, financed by farmers to service agriculture and to help to provide consumers with quality products at fair prices, Dr. Karl D. Butler, Washington, president of the American Institute of Co-operation, told the Ontario Association of Agricultural Societies in Toronto on February 10.
"Farmer co-operatives, as we view them in the United States, are a definite and integral part of the capitalistic system," Dr. Butler said. "Farmers are in business to feed and clothe people and it is their intention to make a living doing it," he said. "This means, in a capitalistic economy, such as we have in the United States and Canada, that they need to operate for a profit."
I think it is well that we understand that, because on the whole co-operatives render splendid service in this country.

It is not in my hands but I think I can guess the date. We know that this government has lost many of the best markets for agricultural products, and that the new incoming government will certainly inherit many real problems, especially with regard to markets, as a result of this administration.
I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, protesting the proposed removal of the T.C.A. headquarters and personnel from

Winnipeg. I am sure that all members, not only from Winnipeg but from the province of Manitoba, have received wires and letters from various organizations protesting this proposed move. May I say that, with respect to geography, the future national defence of the country, and for many other reasons, Winnipeg city is the logical place for the location of the T.C.A. headquarters. Winnipeg is located approximately halfway across the southern part of Canada, and has long been recognized as the gateway between eastern and western Canada. Why it should be proposed to move the headquarters and personnel to either coast is more than I can reason out myself. I sincerely trust the authorities will give every consideration to this problem, and will retain and extend the headquarters in Winnipeg. If certain things happen a few years hence, of which we are rather fearful, I am sure the movement of the headquarters from the city of Winnipeg will be greatly regretted. Many of us have approached the minister in connection with this matter, and he has told us that it is a question of internal administration, but I do hope this government will look into it very carefully before the move is permitted. I am sure all hon. members from the province of Manitoba, irrespective of party, will support the stand I am taking, since any such move will affect many people in Winnipeg and, I think, the system from coast to coast as well. So it is an important problem.
Undoubtedly I shall support the nonconfidence amendment moved this afternoon by my colleague the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). I have already pointed out the situation that will be inherited by the new government that will come into office after the election, as a result of the policies of this administration, irrespective of the budget we have been discussing today.
